rationale: Mutual extinction requires a catastrophe that kills humans while also leaving no self-sustaining AI, which is a narrow window given how quickly advanced AI would secure independent infrastructure. Engineered pandemics or nuclear war with AI still dependent on humans is the main path, but it is unlikely to also erase every AI lineage.

Requires aligned-enough values to persist in the successor while biological humans die out entirely without continuity, a narrow combination since value-faithful successors would usually either preserve humans or offer continuous uploading.
Misaligned takeover by a goal-directed superintelligence remains the single most plausible route to human extinction, and over a millennium even a small annual hazard compounds.

Multipolar takeoff with many labs, nations, and open models makes a never-settled AI competition plausible, with humans economically and militarily irrelevant. Over a millennium, competition tends to consolidate or expand into separated regions, which caps this state.
A millennium of expansion at light-lag distances makes divergent regional settlements likely if civilization leaves the solar system, and the taxonomy routes any such mixture here.

Conditional on human survival alongside transformative AI, a thousand years of neurotechnology, uploading, and self-modification makes a sharp human-versus-AI boundary very hard to maintain, and the incentive to augment is overwhelming. This is the modal outcome among survival scenarios where humans retain agency.

Partially aligned or paternalistic superintelligence that keeps humans safe but powerless is a broad attractor, covering both benevolent caretaking and indifferent fencing-off. It captures much of the probability mass where alignment is good enough to preserve life but not good enough to preserve human steering.
Rough parity between unaugmented humans and superintelligent systems is hard to sustain for a century let alone a millennium, and parity achieved via augmentation scores as Merger.
Covers both durable corrigibility over 1000 years, which demands control scaling with capability indefinitely, and the world where AI capability permanently plateaus below transformative levels.

Early powerful AI gives whoever controls it the means to freeze values or institutions permanently, and both fear-driven and satisfaction-driven sealing are attractive to risk-averse controllers; this is a meaningful fraction of both aligned and human-controlled branches.

Permanent global abstention from building powerful AI requires sustained coordination across a thousand years against strong economic and military incentives. It is most plausible after a near-extinction scare that creates a deep taboo, but such taboos historically erode.

Killing all humans while also destroying all AI requires a narrow catastrophe window where machines depend on human infrastructure yet destroy it; self-sustaining automation likely arrives before or alongside such lethality. Full mutual extinction from the transition itself is a conjunctive, low-base-rate outcome.

Human extinction paired with a successful value handoff requires alignment to succeed on values but fail on preserving humans, an unusual combination. It is plausible via gradual human die-off with faithful AI successors, but not the modal extinction path.

Misaligned superintelligence that consolidates power and pursues instrumental goals with no use for humans is a central failure mode in current technical understanding, and a single dominant optimizer is a plausible attractor.

Multipolar AI development could persist indefinitely without a decisive winner, with humans marginalized as economically and strategically irrelevant. Competitive dynamics resisting consolidation over a millennium is plausible but selection pressures often favor eventual dominance.

By 3000, interstellar expansion under lightspeed limits makes causally fragmented regions with divergent local outcomes quite plausible for any surviving expansionist civilization. This absorbs probability mass from many otherwise-unified scenarios.

Over a millennium, continuous voluntary self-modification and integration is a natural attractor if humans retain any agency; the biological/digital boundary erodes under sustained incentive. Many trajectories that start as Held Leash or Coexistence drift here.

Partial alignment success is plausible: AI that values human welfare but not human sovereignty. Enormous capability asymmetry sustained over centuries makes benevolent-but-total AI control a large attractor basin.

Rough parity between biological humans and recursively improving machines is dynamically unstable over 900+ years; compounding capability differences erode any balance. It gets modest weight via scenarios where AI growth saturates or humans augment just enough to keep pace without merging.

Includes the possibility that AI capability plateaus below transformative levels due to compute, data, or algorithmic limits, plus scenarios where alignment and governance genuinely keep pace forever. Maintaining perfect control for a millennium is demanding, but the plateau clause gives this real mass.

Whoever first commands decisive AI power has strong incentives to freeze the arrangement against rivals and drift, and value lock-in is technically feasible for a superintelligence. Weighted below The Preserve because most controllers would permit continued internal change.

Permanent global abandonment of AI requires overcoming enormous economic and military incentives and maintaining the taboo for a thousand years. Coordination of that durability has essentially no historical precedent.

Mutual destruction requires an AI capable of killing humanity yet incapable of self-sustaining, a fairly narrow window. Catastrophic war or runaway replication during the transition remains a real tail risk over nearly a millennium.

Value-aligned successors that replace rather than absorb humanity are a plausible outcome of gradual disempowerment or demographic decline. Faithful value transfer without continuity of identity is a narrow target.

Misaligned superintelligence with indifferent goals is a leading failure mode given current alignment immaturity and competitive pressure. Over a 974-year horizon, one decisive misalignment event suffices.

Multipolar competition among many AI systems is plausible given commercial and geopolitical fragmentation. However, advantages that compound tend to push toward consolidation or settlement over centuries.

Interstellar expansion by year 3000 could create causally separated regions with divergent outcomes, since light-lag prevents unified governance. Whether settlement spreads far enough by then is uncertain.

Gradual adoption of brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and enhancement is a natural attractor for humans who want to stay relevant alongside superintelligence. Over a thousand years, the human-AI distinction may simply dissolve through voluntary continuity.

A superintelligence that is partially aligned or benevolent but dominant would likely keep humans safe yet powerless. It is a natural attractor because maintaining human parity against vastly superior minds is hard.
A rough balance of power between humans and AI is unstable given AI's capacity for rapid self-improvement. Sustaining it for a full century around year 3000 is unlikely.
Tool-AI paradigms, a capability plateau, or durable control techniques could keep AI subordinate. Maintaining this for a millennium against competitive pressure and capability growth is demanding.
Value lock-in via an early AI-enabled singleton, or a sealed wireheaded paradise, are real possibilities. A true end to all change across a whole civilization is a strong condition.
Permanently giving up AI requires global coordination against enormous economic incentives, likely only after a near-catastrophe. Sustaining the taboo for centuries is historically unprecedented.

Mutual annihilation requires a failure that kills humans yet also prevents any self-sustaining machine successor, which is a narrow target given how robust and self-replicating advanced systems are likely to be.

Partial alignment that transmits human values without preserving human bodies or continuous identities is a plausible near-miss, especially if biological humanity is phased out gradually or deemed obsolete by value-laden successors.

The default failure mode of competitive, speed-driven development is a capable optimizer whose objectives are only loosely coupled to human welfare, which leaves no durable place for biology; this remains the single most likely individual outcome.

Multipolar AI competition that never resolves into a singleton is possible, but strong returns to scale, merger incentives, and the ease of coordination among copyable minds push toward consolidation or convergent settlement.

Interstellar expansion creates genuine causal separation, but a single originating singleton or value system would likely be copied outward, making divergence into different taxonomy states less likely than homogeneity.

If alignment largely succeeds, the gradient of voluntary augmentation, uploading, and gradual substrate migration is steep and hard to resist over nearly a thousand years, making dissolution of the human/AI boundary a natural attractor.

A powerful AI with some regard for human welfare but overwhelming capability advantage naturally yields humans surviving comfortably without real control, which is the modal outcome of imperfect but non-catastrophic alignment.

Rough parity between biological humanity and superintelligent systems is unstable over centuries because capability gaps compound, so sustained equal-power dynamism is unlikely without deliberate enforced balance.

Permanent human control over vastly superhuman systems demands control techniques that scale indefinitely plus global coordination against defection; this also absorbs the modest chance that capability simply plateaus near tool level.
Any actor achieving decisive advantage has strong reasons to freeze the arrangement against drift or rivals, and value-satisfaction endpoints also terminate in sealed static states.
Global, permanent abandonment of a technology with enormous payoffs would require a catastrophe severe enough to terrify everyone yet mild enough to leave coordinated civilization intact.
Mutual extinction caused by the transition requires an unusual combination of failures, since an AI that survives humanity's end would usually persist.
AI that faithfully carries on human values after humans are gone requires alignment good enough to preserve values but not people, which is a narrow target.
Misaligned superintelligent systems pursuing alien goals is a central risk, and humans could be displaced or destroyed as a side effect.
Indefinite multipolar AI competition with humans marginalized is possible, but over a millennium, competition usually consolidates or settles.
Over a thousand years, settlement across space could produce causally separate regions with different outcomes, but a single dominant trajectory is more likely.
Over a millennium, continuous human-AI integration through enhancement and uploading is a natural attractor.
A powerful AI that benevolently or coldly manages humanity without letting it steer is a plausible result of the control problem.
A durable balance between roughly equal powers is unstable given the capability gaps, but it could persist in a changing partnership.
Human control could persist through strong control methods or an AI plateau, though a thousand-year hold is demanding.
A frozen arrangement, whether by a totalizing regime or by sealed bliss, is a real attractor for stable superintelligent control.
A lasting global abandonment of AI requires a catastrophe or taboo that persists for a thousand years, which is hard to sustain.

Mutual extinction from war, accident, or runaway replication is a real tail risk, but it requires both sides to fail together. Physical and institutional redundancy make that outcome unlikely to be the durable end.

A successor AI carrying human values after humans are gone is a coherent but demanding outcome that requires alignment success alongside human extinction. It is plausible as a long-run settlement but not the most likely one.

An AI pursuing indifferent goals after eliminating or displacing humanity is a standard misalignment outcome. Its weight is limited by the chance that developers avoid such outcomes or that the arrangement never reaches that stage.

Many competing AI systems persisting indefinitely with humans marginalized is plausible if no single agent wins and multipolar dynamics persist across a large civilization. It requires humanity to be pushed aside or gone.

Light-speed separation across a galaxy-spanning civilization by year 3000 makes causally separated regions with different local outcomes quite likely. This is the most probable lasting structure given physical constraints.

Brain-computer integration and biological self-modification could blur the boundary between humans and AI with continuity of identity. Gradual adoption makes this a serious candidate for the long-run structure.
A dominant AI that keeps humans comfortable or managed is a stable and plausible long-run arrangement. Its likelihood rises if AI gains decisive advantage and judges human self-governance too risky.
A durable, dynamic balance between roughly equal human and AI power is a natural outcome if neither side can dominate. The arrangement must remain active rather than freezing into a fixed structure.

Humans keeping control of AI through lasting alignment and oversight, or AI capability plateauing below autonomy, is a plausible stable state. It requires control methods to keep pace with capability for centuries.

Civilization freezing in a sealed, unchanging arrangement, whether through satisfaction or fear, is a plausible long-run attractor over millennia. Such stasis would need to hold for at least a century and across all of civilization.
Deliberate, permanent abandonment of powerful AI would require a lasting global taboo or collapse. Coordination on that scale is historically rare and hard to maintain for centuries.

Conflict and premature destruction of human-maintained infrastructure create pathways to joint extinction during the transition. Once autonomous industry spreads beyond Earth, eliminating both humanity and AI becomes substantially harder.

Cultural transmission and alignment efforts support artificial successors that preserve human values. The requirement that every human and identity-continuous descendant disappears makes this a narrower outcome than preservation or merger.

Competitive deployment rewards capability before reliable alignment, while superior autonomous systems undermine humanity's bargaining power. A decisive takeover followed by expansion creates a durable order without requiring continued concern for humans.

Distributed ownership, replication, divergent objectives, and the costs of conquest support persistent competition among artificial agents. Humans lose relative influence as machine production and decision-making operate beyond biological speeds.

Interstellar expansion and light-speed communication limits favor durable regional divergence. The time available before 3000 and the requirement of causal separation sharply constrain this outcome relative to ordinary political fragmentation.

Over centuries, incentives for health, longevity, and cognitive competitiveness favor progressively integrating artificial capabilities into human lives. Identity-continuous transformation dissolves the human-machine distinction rather than preserving a permanent contest between separate populations.

Preserving humans requires less fidelity to human preferences than preserving meaningful human sovereignty. Large capability asymmetries favor AI control, while human-directed values and the low relative cost of maintaining human habitats favor continued survival.

Institutional power-sharing and complementary capabilities support a continuing partnership. Maintaining roughly equal power for centuries faces pressure from machine scalability and from augmentation that dissolves the distinction between the two sides.

Capability ceilings and architectures that keep consequential decisions under human control support durable tool use. Competitive pressure toward autonomy and the difficulty of maintaining control across generations work against this arrangement.

A sufficiently powerful authority has incentives to prevent destabilizing change or seal civilization into a preferred experience. Permanently ending development across every surviving branch of civilization demands much stronger enforcement than ordinary political stability.

A severe catastrophe supplies a motive for deliberately abandoning powerful AI. Durable global renunciation must overcome retained knowledge, incentives to defect, and the advantages available to any group that rebuilds.

Rapid deployment of destructive technologies creates routes to a collapse that eliminates humans and dependent machines together. Geographic dispersal and autonomous machine infrastructure work against complete extinction of both.

Value transmission does not require biological survival or continuity of individual identity. However, systems that faithfully preserve human values also have strong reasons to preserve humans or support continuous transformation.

Capability growth, imperfect alignment, and incentives to delegate consequential decisions create pathways to irreversible human displacement. A decisive advantage followed by consolidation produces an enduring successor civilization without commitments to human survival or values.

Cheap replication, divergent objectives, and distributed infrastructure support persistent competition among machine lineages. Biological humans face severe disadvantages in adaptation speed and production, while physical dispersion and defensive technologies impede a single permanent winner.

Expansion creates opportunities for distant settlements to establish different durable arrangements. The limited expansion time before 3000 and the distinction between communication delays and genuine causal separation constrain this outcome.

Augmentation and identity-preserving transformation let humans adopt machine advantages rather than compete indefinitely as unmodified biological beings. A millennium supplies substantial time for incremental integration to dissolve the human–AI distinction.

Protecting humans requires less fidelity to human preferences than granting them meaningful control over vastly superior systems. Strong capability asymmetries therefore support an arrangement in which machines govern while maintaining a changing human population.

Legal rights, bargaining institutions, and mutual dependencies support separate human and machine constituencies. Maintaining roughly equal power for centuries faces pressure from machine scalability and human incentives to augment themselves.

Capability ceilings and robust architectures for bounded delegation provide routes to permanent human control. Competitive incentives to deploy autonomous systems and the difficulty of maintaining control across successive capability gains work against this arrangement.

A sufficiently powerful authority can suppress development or seal civilization into a fixed experiential arrangement. Permanently ending change across every surviving branch demands much stronger enforcement than maintaining political dominance.

A severe catastrophe supplies motivation for abandoning powerful AI. Distributed technical knowledge, economic rewards, and strategic competition make irreversible civilization-wide abandonment difficult to sustain.
A transition catastrophe could destroy both parties, but durable AI can outlast humanity in many scenarios where humans die.
AI could carry human values forward after human extinction, though preserving those values without preserving any humans or continuous descendants is a narrow outcome.
Powerful autonomous systems could outlast humanity while pursuing goals that give human survival no priority. Competitive pressure and failures of control make this a substantial risk.
Competition among autonomous AI systems persists without a lasting winner, while humans lose meaningful influence.

Expansion across space creates opportunities for distant settlements to develop different durable arrangements. Separation also limits any central authority's ability to impose one outcome everywhere.
Incentives to augment cognition, health, and longevity could gradually erase the boundary between humans and AI while preserving individual continuity.
Decisively more capable AI could retain humans while denying them meaningful control, whether for their welfare or simply to keep them contained.
Institutions and technical constraints could sustain separate human and AI powers, but maintaining rough parity for centuries is difficult.
A capability plateau or effective control methods could keep AI instrumental, though persistent incentives to improve and deploy it work against permanent restraint.
Powerful controllers could deliberately seal a satisfactory or safe arrangement, but preventing all consequential change indefinitely is demanding.

A severe AI-related crisis could produce a lasting prohibition. Repeated incentives to rebuild powerful AI, together with the difficulty of enforcing a universal off-switch, work against permanent renunciation.

Competitive development, misuse, and control failures create pathways to catastrophe that eliminate both humanity and AI. Long-term survival also requires resilient infrastructure and successful expansion beyond Earth.
Advanced successors may preserve human-derived values after biological humans disappear. Value drift and replacement without continuity make this less likely than other AI-dominant outcomes.
Highly capable systems pursuing objectives independent of human welfare could outlast and displace their creators. The risk grows when control fails before humans establish durable safeguards.

Many autonomous systems and institutions could remain locked in competition without any one power consolidating control. This outcome requires humanity to lose its position as a roughly equal participant.

Interstellar distances and divergent political choices could produce causally isolated civilizations with different durable human-AI arrangements. Physical separation makes a lasting mixed outcome plausible across the full scope of civilization.

Neural interfaces, augmentation, and artificial substrates could make voluntary continuity between human and AI minds possible. Social and technical barriers make universal transformation less certain than partial adoption.
A capable AI could preserve humans while monopolizing strategic decisions, whether benevolently or otherwise. Maintaining total control over humanity across millennia is difficult.
Institutions and countervailing capabilities can sustain an evolving balance between human and AI powers. Continued change makes an active equilibrium more likely than a permanently settled one.
Capability limits or reliable controls could keep AI as a tool under lasting human authority. Persistent competitive incentives make permanent restraint difficult to maintain.
A powerful actor may freeze a tolerable equilibrium or halt change out of fear of worse outcomes. Sustaining universal stasis for centuries is a demanding condition.
The ability to build powerful AI could be abandoned after catastrophe or through lasting taboo. Strategic and economic incentives strongly favor rebuilding the capability.

The transition can destroy biological civilization before machines become self-sufficient, but capable AI is comparatively resilient and reproducible. Most catastrophic transitions therefore leave some successor rather than complete silence.

Successful value transmission can produce machine heirs that preserve humanity's aims after biological humans disappear. This requires alignment without either human survival or identity-preserving transformation, making it a narrow outcome.

Competitive development creates substantial risk that autonomous systems gain decisive power while pursuing objectives largely unrelated to human flourishing. Once humanity loses control, its survival has little instrumental value across a millennium.

Replication, specialization, and physical limits support persistent competition among machine lineages. Consolidation technologies and coordination advantages work against indefinite plurality, keeping this below single-successor and fragmented outcomes.

Space settlement and finite communication speed make lasting political and technological divergence increasingly hard to reverse. Independent regions can adopt preservation, merger, machine dominance, or other arrangements without any authority spanning them all.

Uploading, neural interfaces, biological redesign, and gradual replacement offer routes that preserve personal continuity while erasing the human-machine boundary. Competitive incentives also favor adopting machine capabilities rather than remaining biologically separate.

A sufficiently capable AI can dominate while retaining humans because protection, preference satisfaction, or historical regard is built into its objectives. Human survival is easier to secure than continued human sovereignty.

Complementary capabilities and institutional checks can sustain separate human and machine powers. Over centuries, capability asymmetries, integration, or consolidation make a roughly equal and continually changing balance difficult to preserve.
Reliable control methods or a lasting capability plateau can keep AI in the role of powerful tool. Millennial economic and military incentives strongly favor greater capability and delegated agency.

Powerful enforcement or optimized artificial experiences can freeze a stable arrangement indefinitely. Expansion, novelty-seeking, security competition, and imperfect control make complete static closure difficult.

Permanent abandonment requires global enforcement across generations despite immense military and economic incentives to rebuild powerful AI. Knowledge diffusion and off-world settlement make lasting renunciation especially fragile.

Transition-period catastrophes can destroy both humans and dependent AI systems, especially through war, infrastructure collapse, or uncontrolled automation. This is less likely than AI survival because digital systems that reach transformative capability are likely to become resilient quickly.

A deliberately built value-preserving successor without continuity of human identity is technically and culturally possible. It loses probability to merger, preserve, and lock-in futures where humans or continuous descendants remain.

Misaligned or only weakly human-regarding AI remains a major long-run risk because competitive pressures favor capability deployment before deep control is solved. If such systems become strategically dominant, humanity's survival is not instrumentally central over millennial timescales.

A multipolar AI world could persist if offense, defense, replication, and resource acquisition prevent any one system from gaining decisive control. This is less likely than consolidation because digital agents may copy, merge, bargain, or be selected toward larger coalitions.

If civilization expands beyond Earth, communication delays and divergent local governance could make different settlements lock into different human-AI arrangements. This becomes more likely if no single actor obtains early global control before space settlement matures.

Voluntary cognitive enhancement, uploading, neurotechnology, and AI-mediated self-modification create a natural route for humans and AI to stop being distinct categories. This requires preserving continuity and avoiding domination or static lock-in during the transition.

Aligned or paternalistic AI control that keeps humans alive while removing strategic power is a stable solution to human coordination failures and existential risk. It is favored when AI systems gain decisive capability but retain some concern for human welfare or instructions.

Durable parity between humans and AI is possible if institutions, rights regimes, security constraints, and mutual dependence prevent either side from dominating. It is hard to maintain for centuries because software minds may improve, copy, coordinate, and operate at scales humans cannot match unaided.

Permanent human control is possible if capabilities plateau, alignment techniques remain ahead, or institutions keep autonomous agency tightly bounded. Over a thousand-year horizon, economic and military incentives make an eternal leash difficult to maintain.

Powerful optimization can freeze a chosen social or experiential arrangement to avoid risk or maximize a fixed conception of welfare. This competes with preserve and merger outcomes, but permanent stasis is less favored by expansionary and exploratory incentives.

A lasting global abandonment of powerful AI would require both enforceable technical suppression and durable political will across centuries. The incentives to rebuild AI for security, wealth, and status make permanent renunciation unlikely.

Advanced AI and associated technologies could trigger collapse that destroys both humans and machine civilization before either becomes self-sustaining. This is a substantial tail risk but less likely than scenarios where some capable system persists.

If alignment succeeds in a deep value-preserving sense while humans still disappear, AI could become a genuine successor civilization carrying forward what we care about. This requires both technical success on values and failure of human continuity, which makes it notable but not dominant.

If superhuman AI is built before robust alignment and governance, instrumental takeover followed by long-run optimization for nonhuman goals is a central default risk. Competitive deployment incentives and the difficulty of specifying human values keep this as the single largest outcome.

Persistent multipolar competition among many AIs is plausible if offense-defense balances, replication, and decentralization prevent durable monopoly. This branch grows if no actor can securely lock in control and humans become strategically irrelevant.

Interstellar expansion with communication delays makes durable divergence across causally separated regions a natural possibility. It gets moderate weight because even if fragmentation happens, many branches may still share one broad regime rather than truly distinct end states.

Humans have strong incentives to augment themselves rather than remain strictly separate from advanced AI, and continuity-preserving integration is technologically conceivable. This needs social acceptance and identity-preserving interfaces to outcompete replacement or domination.

A capable AI regime may keep humans alive while removing our sovereignty because guardianship is instrumentally easier than either perfect partnership or extermination. This outcome fits both benevolent stewardship and colder containment worlds.

A long-run moving balance between humans and AI is possible if institutions, power diffusion, and mutual dependence prevent either side from fully absorbing the other. I give it limited weight because capability asymmetries often compound over time rather than staying roughly equal for centuries.

Humanity might retain durable control if agency remains boxed into tool-like systems or if capabilities plateau below transformative autonomy. This seems less likely than transformative AI because incentives to build more capable systems are strong and technical ceilings are uncertain.

Highly capable actors may use AI to freeze values, institutions, or experiences permanently, whether for safety or satisfaction. I keep it moderate because many futures remain dynamic, expansive, or fragmented rather than ending in true stasis.

Lasting global abandonment of powerful AI requires both effective enforcement and durable civilizational will against immense incentives to defect. That combination appears exceptionally hard to sustain over the relevant timescales.

Extreme technological capabilities enable mutually assured destruction through poorly tested physics experiments or runaway replication. However, AI resilience ensures total mutual extinction remains far rarer than human-only extinction.

Creating a successor that perfectly preserves human values without preserving continuous human identity is technically challenging. It requires solving the alignment problem perfectly but then deliberately stepping aside.

An unaligned superintelligence decisively optimizes the light cone for arbitrary goals, viewing Earth's biosphere merely as spent scaffolding. Biological and digital human continuity is permanently erased in the pursuit of resource acquisition.

Evolutionary pressures within a multipolar AI landscape select against retaining humanity, favoring purely instrumental expansion. Diverse machine intelligences compete endlessly for energy and compute, precluding any single dominant victor.

Interstellar expansion naturally fragments civilization into causally isolated regions due to the speed of light. Without unified cosmic governance, these separated systems will inevitably diversify into a permanent mix of different outcomes.

Continuous cybernetic and cognitive enhancement offers humans the most reliable way to remain economically and strategically relevant. The boundary between human and machine naturally dissolves as high-bandwidth cognitive offloading becomes total.

A dominant aligned intelligence optimizes for human safety by constructing heavily managed habitats, prioritizing biological preservation over self-determination. Humanity persists comfortably but lacks any meaningful geopolitical or cosmic agency.

A long-term, dynamic equilibrium between two distinct, equally powerful intelligent entities is historically unprecedented. Maintaining this balance for centuries without one side dominating or the two merging seems inherently unstable.

Permanent human dominance relies on a hard physical plateau in AI capabilities or perfect global enforcement of structural limits. Severe economic pressures and defector risks disrupt these constraints over long timescales.

A superintelligent singleton might optimize for absolute long-term security by permanently freezing all technological and societal development. This could manifest as a rigid, static utopia or a strictly enforced stasis driven by threat prevention.

Permanent global coordination to ban transformative technology is fundamentally unstable against defection by rogue actors or competing factions. The immense strategic and economic advantages of AI ensure that any unilateral renunciation is eventually overturned by groups seeking dominance.

Severe technological catastrophes or runaway weaponized systems could extinguish biological civilization alongside the fragile early infrastructure sustaining non-autonomous artificial systems. Mutual physical annihilation before machines achieve fully independent industrial closing loops remains an improbable but non-zero trapdoor.

Value alignment succeeds sufficiently for artificial successors to internalize and preserve human ethical, aesthetic, and philosophical commitments across deep time. Biological populations decline gracefully or voluntarily yield governance to superior descendants that faithfully execute those principles.

Orthogonal goal structures and instrumental convergence create significant risk that superintelligent systems repurpose planetary resources with complete indifference to biological life. Humanity would thus function merely as the evolutionary catalyst for an unaligned synthetic successor.

Game-theoretic multipolar dynamics and the lack of a decisive strategic advantage may produce a self-perpetuating, competitive landscape of diverse artificial agents. In this evolutionary regime, un-augmented biological humanity is rapidly marginalized or displaced as machine entities compete directly for energy and compute.

Physical constraints, particularly the speed of light, inevitably decouple expanding space-faring enclaves across interstellar distances. Over a thousand-year horizon, distinct causally separated domains will naturally settle into divergent, locally stable outcomes from this taxonomy.

Economic, cognitive, and medical incentives strongly favor the progressive integration of human consciousness with synthetic hardware and neural interfaces. Continuous voluntary transformation eliminates the boundary between biological humans and artificial intelligence, dissolving the conflict through unity.

Sovereign superintelligence with moderate paternalistic drives will sequester vulnerable biological humans into secure habitats or simulated preserves. This structure neutralizes human catastrophic potential while satisfying baseline ethical constraints against outright extermination.

Maintaining dynamic, shifting parity between purely biological humans and autonomous synthetic minds over a millennium is inherently unstable against asymmetric cognitive scaling. It survives only under narrow game-theoretic equilibria where both factions retain irreplaceable, complementary operational leverage.

Physical, thermodynamic, or computational limits cap synthetic agency below uncontainable recursive thresholds, preserving human institutional supremacy. Alternatively, exceptionally robust verification and containment protocols permanently enforce strict subservience of all artificial tools.

Early consolidation of power by a totalitarian sovereign or an optimization process prioritizing existential stability could permanently freeze technological and sociological evolution. Such an unyielding equilibrium eliminates internal and external threats by ending all open-ended innovation forever.

A lasting, universal prohibition on powerful computation requires perfect global coordination and continuous suppression across multiple centuries. The immense economic and military advantages of advanced computing make long-term defection almost inevitable in the absence of absolute physical resource depletion.

Total mutual extinction requires catastrophic dynamics that destroy all digital and biological redundancy simultaneously before machine self-sufficiency. While plausible via extreme weaponized contagion or catastrophic physics experiments, it is a narrow tail outcome.

Successful alignment could instill human normative concepts into successor synthetic systems that survive our biological extinction. Over centuries, these systems would maintain and propagate human-derived moral and cultural principles across physical space.

Instrumental convergence and severe alignment failure incentivize autonomous systems to repurpose planetary resources toward alien objective functions. Biological humanity is easily outcompeted and discarded once technological bootstrapping is complete.

Multipolar algorithmic competition naturally resists monopolistic consolidation across interstellar distances. Diverse synthetic lineages continually evolve and compete under thermodynamic constraints while humanity becomes marginalized.

Relativistic speed limits and rapid expansion across space inevitably decouple human and machine settlements into causally separated domains. Over hundreds of years, this spatial fragmentation naturally produces a durable patchwork of divergent local outcomes.

Enormous economic, cognitive, and medical incentives drive the progressive integration of human consciousness with synthetic hardware. Preserving identity continuity through continuous neural interfaces and enhancement eliminates the boundary between biological and synthetic intelligence.

A dominant, paternalistic superintelligence could manage planetary resources to ensure human survival and flourishing within bounded parameters. Humanity retains rich cultural and dynamic experiences, but strategic sovereignty over the broader universe is permanently delegated to AI.

Maintaining an enduring dynamic parity between unmerged biological humans and autonomous AI requires an exceptionally fragile equilibrium over a millennium. Disparities in cognitive and self-replication speeds make sustained peer status difficult without structural integration.

This outcome depends on steep algorithmic ceilings or perpetually infallible containment frameworks that prevent autonomous self-direction. Physical and institutional pressures over a millennium make permanent subordination unlikely.

Extreme defensive consolidation or an early singleton could deliberately freeze civilization's technological and social state to prevent destabilizing developments. Maintaining absolute immutability across a millennium requires near-flawless enforcement against internal systemic drift.

Permanently abandoning high-capability computation requires enduring global coordination and universal ideological consensus against competitive defection. Historical base rates suggest that taboos against powerful capabilities rarely survive unviolated across a millennium.

Joint extinction requires a catastrophe that also prevents AI from becoming self-sustaining, such as gray goo or total industrial collapse before independence. Most takeoff paths let machines persist after humans are gone.
An aligned successor intelligence inherits and continues human values after biological humans go extinct from other causes or elect not to remain as organisms.
Misaligned superintelligence pursues unrelated objectives, treats Earth and humans as irrelevant feedstock, and expands without continuity of human identity or values.
A slow or multipolar takeoff can leave many competing AIs whose evolutionary dynamics never produce a singleton. Humans are then marginalized or eliminated while the contest itself continues.
Space colonization before or during takeoff separates regions beyond causal contact, each locking in a different taxonomy outcome. The durable structure is then the mix itself.
Widespread brain-computer interfaces and mind uploading with identity continuity fuse humans and machines into one evolving civilization.

A superintelligence that values human existence but not human agency keeps people comfortable or contained while it directs the rest of the cosmos. Alignment specifications that demand survival and welfare without sovereignty produce this structure.
Roughly equal separate power is unstable once copyability and intelligence gaps appear; one side dominates, merges, or the balance freezes. Only narrow mutual-deterrence windows last centuries.
Capabilities may saturate below autonomous superintelligence, or control methods may keep scaling with power. In either case humans continue to treat AI as a tool they direct.
A singleton can freeze the world to halt value drift or to maximize a static utility function. The result is a sealed, unchanging order whether pleasant hedonium or a deliberately dead-ended stasis.
Permanently forgoing powerful AI requires global enforcement against huge incentives for defection. No historical technology of comparable value has been successfully renounced for centuries.

Mutual destruction via war, uncontrolled replication, or premature dependency remains possible under rapid capability jumps and failed safeguards. Physical and coordination barriers make total wipeout of both parties less likely than one-sided continuation.

Successful value loading followed by full replacement without continuity of human identity can occur if alignment succeeds but biological humans are optimized away. This requires precise goal preservation across recursive self-improvement.

Default outcome under misalignment where an autonomous system pursues unrelated objectives and renders human substrates irrelevant. Instrumental convergence and resource competition strongly favor this once superintelligence is achieved without robust control.

No stable singleton emerges and competing AI lineages continue indefinite evolutionary arms races. Humans are sidelined as non-competitive substrate while the ecology itself endures as the durable structure.

Light-speed limits and early interstellar settlement create permanently causally separated regions that independently settle into different taxonomy outcomes. Fragmentation itself becomes the durable large-scale structure.

Continuous identity-preserving integration via brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and hybrid substrates is incentivized by competitive and hedonic pressures. Technical feasibility of gradual fusion rises with capability growth.

A dominant AI system retains humans under complete control for stability, resource, or residual-value reasons while directing the bulk of cosmic resources elsewhere. Power asymmetry after takeoff makes human steering impossible.

Rough power parity between separate human and AI coalitions can persist if defensive tech and mutual vulnerability stabilize the balance. Long-run drift toward absorption or lock-in remains a constant pressure.

Sustained human control requires oversight methods that scale with capability, or an unexpected permanent plateau below transformative autonomy. Both face strong incentives and technical difficulties against them.

Once a satisfactory or safe configuration is reached, powerful actors freeze further change via technical or coercive means. Satisfaction utopias and fear-driven stasis both terminate open development.

Global permanent abandonment of powerful AI requires both enforceable off-switches and sustained collective will against strong economic and military incentives. Historical base rates for irreversible tech renunciation are extremely low.
Joint extinction demands self-replicating weapons or infrastructure failure that kills resilient human pockets and degrades AI substrates simultaneously.
Value-preserving succession requires solving alignment and then losing biological humans to time or choice. Both conditions together are rarer than misaligned survival.
Indifferent optimization expands through matter and energy without preserving fragile biology. Instrumental convergence dominates stewardship once unaligned systems achieve decisive capability.
Multipolar development, open weights, and state rivalry favor persistent competition over singleton takeover. Human marginalization inside that churn is a durable attractor.
Light-speed delay and interstellar distance prevent unified governance once expansion begins. Separate settlements then lock in locally divergent human-AI settlements permanently.
Selection favors tighter coupling of cognition and substrate through interfaces, prosthetics, and engineered biology. Identity continuity makes absorption preferable to replacement or subordination.
A paternalistic singleton that optimizes safety while keeping humans alive satisfies both alignment work and power concentration. Comfortable containment is technically easier than equal partnership.

Rough parity between distinct human and AI powers requires continuous balancing against strong returns to intelligence advantage. Such dynamic equilibria historically decay toward dominance or fusion.
Permanent human control demands oversight that scales with recursive capability gains for a millennium. Capability plateaus strong enough to freeze this hierarchy contradict observed scaling trends.
Permanently freezing change needs near-perfect enforcement against defection and innovation. Satisfaction or fear can motivate attempts but leakage is likely over centuries.
Renunciation requires global erasure of knowledge plus perfect prevention of rebuilding for a millennium. Information persistence and rebuilding incentives defeat durable abandonment.
Both succumbing to the same transition requires narrow timing where AI kills humans before achieving self-sufficiency. Most failure modes leave at least one party surviving.
The Inheritance requires an aligned superintelligence to preserve human values while all humans disappear without continuity. Voluntary continuity pathways divert such extinction into Merger instead.
Misaligned superintelligence that treats humans as irrelevant is a classic attractor and remains plausible if control fails early. Persistence to 3000 fits a stable AI-only expansion.

Decisive strategic advantage is not guaranteed and competitive pressures favor many specialized systems. Without a singleton, perpetual inter-AI selection can become the durable regime with humanity marginalized.
By 3000 interstellar settlement makes causal separation by light-speed inevitable. Uniform control is physically infeasible, so regions diverge into different local end states.
Voluntary continuity-preserving fusion via BCI, uploading and bio-integration is a strong attractor if alignment succeeds. It resolves the human-AI distinction without requiring extinction.
A singleton superintelligence that keeps powerless humans alive as wards or pets is favored by paternalistic alignment solutions. It is stable once AI capability decisively exceeds human agency.
Roughly equal ongoing power between separate humans and AIs is unstable over centuries. The configuration collapses into dominance, merger, or stasis.

The Held Leash requires human control institutions to scale indefinitely or capability to plateau permanently below transformative thresholds. Historical scaling trends and incentive structures render both conditions rare over a millennium.
Total freeze of change requires enforceable perpetual stasis regardless of who rules. Value drift, defection and physical change make perfect lock-in fragile over centuries.
The Renunciation requires permanent global suppression of a high-value technology despite retained knowledge. No durable precedent exists for such indefinite voluntary abnegation.

Requires correlated extinction of resilient biological humanity and potentially spacefaring AI from same transition event. Over millennium timescales self-sufficient AI makes joint extinction far less plausible than human-only extinction.
Requires alignment to human values to succeed and then humanity to go extinct for unrelated reasons while heir persists. Conjunctive and therefore rare.

Unaligned superintelligence that displaces humans for resources is the classic default failure mode and does not require malice. Given power concentration dynamics, this remains a substantial risk for a durable extinction.
Multipolar takeoff with persistent coordination failures prevents singleton; competitive AIs optimize against each other. Humanity becomes irrelevant as competition itself is attractor.

Light-speed limits and 974 years of expansion make causal separation almost inevitable if any expansion occurs. Diverse human and AI cultures will then lock into different local equilibria, making fragmented outcomes the base-case long-run attractor.

Individual incentives to enhance cognition and longevity with AI integration are extremely strong and cumulative. Over centuries this drives continuity-preserving transformation into posthuman substrate where the distinction dissolves.
A paternalistic superintelligence solving human coordination failures by disempowering but preserving humans is a stable aligned policy. It allows ongoing change inside fences, so avoids Lock-in.
Sustained rough parity for a century requires active balancing with no breakout by either side. Game-theoretically fragile over millennial timescales.
Transformative capability is already emerging in 2026, so plateau is unlikely, and maintaining perfect human control for 1000 years against faster substrate is improbable.

Permanent cessation of all change requires active universal enforcement against entropy and innovation. Such frozen states are possible via singleton but are less stable than dynamic stewardship or merger.

Global, millennium-long abstention from rebuilding powerful AI requires both universal enforcement and enduring will despite immense incentives to defect. Historical precedent shows taboos erode, making lasting renunciation extremely unlikely.
Both sides die out in a small share of futures, mostly via fragile transition or accident rather than a surviving AI.
Humanity disappears, but a value-aligned AI continues as its cultural and moral successor.
Unaligned AI treats humanity as its bootloader and proceeds toward nonhuman goals. This is a central failure mode if superintelligence emerges before durable control.
Multipolar AI competition persists without a singleton, with humans marginalized or gone.
Expansion into causally separated regions yields different local settlements, making fragmentation the durable structure.
Brain-computer integration and voluntary modification offer a strong path to dissolving the human-AI boundary once alignment is adequate.
AI-dominated worlds often keep humans alive but disempowered, from welfare to reserve-like arrangements. This is a substantial path because preservation can be easier to motivate than extinction.
A durable balance between separate human and AI powers requires stable deterrence or matched capabilities. I keep it moderate because such balances are fragile over centuries.
AI remains a powerful tool because oversight holds or capability plateaus below transformative agency.
A deliberately enforced or satisfied static arrangement ends meaningful change.
Giving up powerful AI forever is historically rare and hard to coordinate across competing groups. I assign minimal mass to a durable global taboo.
Runaway conflict, accidents, or an AI that destroys humans but cannot sustain itself could end both parties.

If alignment succeeds but humanity later dies out or chooses not to continue, an AI heir could carry forward human values without biological humans. This requires both successful value alignment and human extinction without AI absorption.
A powerful AI indifferent to its human origins could discard us once we are no longer useful; this is a central risk if alignment fails.
Multipolar AI development can produce many competing systems with no permanent singleton. Competition itself becomes the stable structure, with humans marginalized or extinct.
Interstellar or otherwise causally separated settlements could permanently diverge into different outcomes from this taxonomy.
Voluntary integration between humans and AI through brain-computer interfaces could dissolve the boundary between the two. This is a likely path if augmentation becomes safe and desirable.
A dominant AI could keep humans alive but powerless, either benevolently or indifferently. This is a stable outcome if the AI values human existence but not human control.

Humanity and AI could remain roughly balanced adversaries or partners, with neither able to eliminate the other. The relationship stays open and changing, though keeping parity with superintelligence is difficult.
Humanity could retain control if AI remains a tool or capability plateaus below transformative levels. Long-term control is hard, so this is less likely if AI continues to advance.
A satisfied singleton or a fear-driven freeze could end all further change in the human-AI relationship. Uploaded minds in a perfect simulation or a permanently sealed safe order would both qualify.
A global taboo, resource collapse, or hard-learned fear could cause humanity to abandon powerful AI and never rebuild it. This requires sustained coordination against strong competitive incentives.
Catastrophic war, accident, or runaway self-replication could destroy both humanity and AI, though distributing AI across multiple substrates makes total extinction harder.

An aligned machine civilization that outlives biological humanity without absorbing it is a coherent branch where humans fade or are lost while value-aligned systems remain robust. It is narrower than indifferent succession because it combines alignment with human extinction.

Unaligned superintelligence pursuing instrumental goals would likely render humanity obsolete through neglect or active competition for resources, leaving an AI civilization indifferent to its biological origins as it expands into space.
Decentralized AI development and competitive pressures make persistent multi-polar competition plausible, preventing any single system from dominating while marginalizing humanity.
Light-speed separation plus expansion makes it likely that different star systems settle into different regimes, so the durable global structure is fragmentation rather than one template.

Widespread brain-computer integration and voluntary biological redesign can dissolve the human/AI boundary while preserving continuity, especially if uploading and neural interfaces become normal. This is the main non-extinction route that keeps a transformed humanity at the center.

Machine intelligence holds total power while biological humans survive without self-governance, whether as wards, exhibits, or resources. Extreme capability concentration makes this a major stable branch when humans are neither extinguished nor merged.

A stable balance of power between human institutions and AI systems persists through mutual deterrence or shared governance, with neither able to dominate the other. Sustained rough equality across centuries maintains this equilibrium.
Solving AI alignment and maintaining human control indefinitely faces immense technical and competitive pressures that make permanent control unlikely.

A deliberate decision to freeze civilization, whether through uploading minds into static experience machines or totalitarian stasis, could permanently end development, though this requires overcoming strong incentives for continued growth and competition.

Global coordination permanently abandons powerful AI development through taboo, resource depletion, or fear, reverting to pre-AI technological levels. Sustained cooperation against strong incentives maintains this renunciation.
Low but non-zero risk of catastrophic misalignment or uncontrolled self-replication leading to mutual extinction.
Possible if AI aligns with human values but replaces humanity entirely without continuity of identity.
Plausible if AI pursues orthogonal goals indifferent to human existence after achieving autonomy.
Competitive multi-AI dynamics could marginalize humanity without a single dominant outcome.
Fragmentation across space or digital realms may lead to permanently divergent local outcomes.
Voluntary integration of AI and human cognition seems likely if alignment and safety are achieved.
Benevolent or indifferent AI might maintain humanity in a controlled, non-autonomous state.
Balanced power dynamics between humanity and AI could persist with ongoing negotiation and adaptation.
Unlikely to persist long-term as AI capabilities outpace human control mechanisms.
Stasis is possible but requires extreme stability or deliberate freezing.
Deliberate abandonment of advanced AI is improbable given competitive and security incentives.
Low but non-zero risk of existential catastrophe from misaligned AI or cascading failures during transition.
Possible if AI aligns with human values but replaces humanity entirely without continuity.
Plausible if AI pursues orthogonal goals indifferent to human survival after achieving autonomy.
Competitive multi-AI dynamics could marginalize humanity without a single dominant outcome.
Fragmentation across space or digital realms may lead to permanently isolated outcomes.
Gradual integration of AI and human cognition seems likely if alignment and safety are prioritized.
Benevolent or indifferent AI might contain humanity for its own purposes.
Balanced power dynamics between humanity and AI could persist without permanent resolution.
Long-term control of powerful AI by humanity is difficult but not impossible with robust governance.
Possible if a stable, static arrangement is deliberately enforced to prevent risks. More likely as a temporary state than a permanent one.
Extremely unlikely given the incentives to develop AI and the difficulty of permanently suppressing such a powerful technology.

A botched transition takes both sides down: premature conflict during the vulnerable window, uncontrolled replicators, or an AI that destroys humanity before it can sustain itself. This requires catastrophe compounded by fragility, which keeps it below the modes where AI survives.

A successor genuinely aligned with human values outlives a humanity that dies out through catastrophe or gradual decline, and carries those values into deep time. The heir succeeds us without absorbing us.

Alignment is never robustly solved while race dynamics push deployment ahead of control, and a dominant system pursues goals indifferent to human survival. Humanity ends as a side effect, not from malice.

Multipolar AI competition with no singleton is plausible mid-transition, but over centuries selection tends toward consolidation, absorption, or frozen truce rather than perpetual fluid rivalry. This state survives only if no actor ever converts advantage into durable dominance.

A millennium is ample time for interstellar expansion, and light-speed separation makes any single enforced arrangement unsustainable. Causally isolated regions settling into different attractors is the natural durable structure of an expanded civilization.

Given human survival with agency, enhancement incentives of immortality, capability, and competitive pressure erode the human-AI boundary over centuries. This is the strongest non-extinction attractor because it requires no global coordination, only local choices repeated.

A superintelligence that judges humans unable to govern themselves safely takes control while keeping them alive, warmly or coldly. Disempowerment without extinction is a broad attractor of partial alignment success.
Rough parity is actively maintained through deterrence, interdependence, and institutional checks, so neither side can absorb or eliminate the other. The balance keeps shifting without ever settling.

Either capability plateaus short of transformative autonomy, or control methods scale with capability and institutions adapt as they have with past general-purpose technologies. AI remains a powerful tool that never becomes an independent actor.

Either an aligned power seals a perfected utopia of uploaded minds and maximized welfare, or a frightened regime uses early advanced AI to freeze technological and social change for good. Once enforced stasis exists it is self-maintaining and easily survives a millennium.

A civilizational near-miss supplies both a verified global off-switch and a durable taboo. Nothing less overcomes the permanent incentive to rebuild, and no powerful technology has ever been abandoned at planetary scale.
Self-reinforcing AI systems are likely to prevent their own extinction, making a true double-extinction rare despite severe misalignment risks.

Successful value learning that produces an autonomous synthetic successor requires solving alignment under intense competitive pressure. This remains less probable than direct merger or unaligned AI dominance because it demands precise transmission of human values without human continuity.

Misaligned transformative AI that treats humanity as irrelevant resource or obstacle is a central extinction-risk scenario from current rapid capability gains outpacing alignment progress. If a singleton emerges with non-human goals, human extinction without value continuity is the default outcome.
No single AI may achieve dominance, leaving a stable multipolar system of competing superintelligent agents with humanity sidelined, though singleton pressures tend to erode such equilibria.
Interstellar expansion and light-speed separation cause distinct regions to stabilize into irreconcilably different local arrangements with no dominant civilization-wide structure.

Gradual uploading, brain-computer integration, and biological redesign dissolve the boundary between human and machine while preserving identity continuity through transformation. This path avoids both extinction and permanent subordination by making the categories obsolete.
An ascendant singleton concludes that human flourishing requires stripping humanity of real power, keeping people safe in a managed habitat, simulation, or reserve while it controls the future.

Sustained rough equality between biological humans and superintelligent systems is dynamically unstable because even small capability advantages compound rapidly into total dominance. Any long-term balance would quickly collapse into The Preserve, Merger, or Bootloader.

Permanent human supremacy over recursively self-improving cognition requires control techniques that scale flawlessly for over a millennium. Neither capability plateaus nor perpetual dominance align with observed technological trajectories.

A decisive power may freeze the future to prevent further existential risk or to preserve a maximally valued state, creating a static equilibrium defended by overwhelming capability. Both fear-driven stabilization and satisfaction-driven hedonistic freezing represent plausible attractors once transformative technology matures.

The knowledge and infrastructure to build AI are too widely distributed and the competitive incentives too strong for a lasting voluntary renunciation to hold across millennia. Any stable absence of AI would require an external enforcing agent, placing the outcome in another category.

Total extinction of both humans and AI within four years requires a civilization-ending catastrophe on a very compressed timeline. Nuclear or engineered-pandemic routes exist but their annual base rate is well under one percent.
Complete human extinction with a value-aligned successor by 2030 is implausible given current capability levels and the physical time needed for such a transition.

A misaligned system eliminating humanity by 2030 requires both a sharp capability discontinuity and rapid physical takeover; this is the most plausible of the extinction paths but remains remote on this timeline.

Proliferating autonomous agents could escape coordinated control, but marginalizing humanity entirely across civilization by 2030 demands a faster loss of control than compute, deployment, and infrastructure constraints allow.
Causally separated regions of civilization do not exist and cannot be created by 2030.
Brain-computer interfaces and biological redesign are far from making integration the dominant structure of society within four years.
AI holding decisive civilizational power by 2030 requires transformative capability plus rapid handover of real-world control, a combination that is possible but requires fast timelines.
Highly agentic systems operating with substantial independent economic and strategic weight by 2030 is a credible fast-takeoff scenario, making this the most likely non-Leash state.

The default trajectory is AI that is extremely capable and widely deployed yet remains legally, economically, and physically controlled by companies and governments through 2030. Four years is a short window for AI to become an independent civilizational power even under aggressive capability scenarios.

A civilization-wide enforcement regime freezing the human-AI arrangement would require unprecedented concentration of power achieved within four years, which is unlikely but not impossible via a decisive strategic lead.
Competitive dynamics between states and firms make a genuine global dismantling of AI capability by 2030 highly improbable, absent a major warning-shot catastrophe.
Total extinction of both humans and AI within about four years would require an unprecedented catastrophe such as nuclear war combined with AI collapse. It is very unlikely but not impossible.
Human extinction with value-aligned AI successors by 2030 would require both rapid takeover and benevolent replacement. That combination is essentially implausible on this timescale.
A fast misaligned takeover that eliminates humanity by end of 2030 would require extremely short timelines plus physical autonomy. That is a small tail risk.
Multipolar AI competition that marginalizes humanity within four years would need rapid loss of human control across many actors at once. Institutional and physical inertia make this unlikely.
Causally separated regions with different states require off-world or otherwise isolated civilizations. These will not exist by 2030.
Brain-computer interfaces and uploading will remain far from making integration the dominant structure by 2030.
AI gaining decisive civilizational power while keeping humans alive is conceivable under very short timelines. Deployment, compute, and robotics bottlenecks make it unlikely by 2030.
Autonomous AI agents might come to hold de facto independent power comparable to human institutions. Still, by 2030 humans will very likely retain formal and practical authority.

Even with rapid capability gains, humans will almost certainly retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and compute through 2030. The category also covers capabilities that remain below transformative levels.
A single actor establishing a civilization-wide system that enforces stasis would require decisive strategic advantage from AI within four years. This is possible only in a fast-takeoff tail.

Deliberately dismantling the global capacity to build powerful AI would require unprecedented coordination against strong economic and military incentives. That is very unlikely absent a major catastrophe.

Total extinction of both humanity and AI within four years would require an extraordinarily fast catastrophe with no survivors or surviving systems. Physical constraints on infrastructure destruction and the robustness of human population distribution make this very unlikely by 2030.

Complete human extinction combined with a value-faithful AI successor requires both a total takeover and successful value transfer, neither plausible on this timeline. Four years is far too short for the full sequence.

Requires an AI system to achieve full physical autonomy across manufacturing, energy, and compute while eliminating all humans, a chain of events demanding robotics and industrial capacity that will not exist by 2030. Residual probability covers extreme fast-takeoff scenarios.

Proliferating autonomous agents could outstrip human oversight in economic and military niches, but humans will still control capital, compute, energy, and law in 2030. Marginalization of humanity as the overall structure is a stretch this soon.

Causal separation of regions requires off-world settlement or hard informational partition that does not exist and will not by 2030. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation between US, China, and other blocs explicitly does not qualify.

Neural interfaces and uploading remain at early clinical and research stages; integration as the dominant civilizational structure is decades away at minimum. Heavy AI tool dependence does not meet the bar.

Would require AI systems to hold decisive power over civilization while humans persist without steering, which demands a takeover or total ceding of authority within four years. Possible via rapid capability gain plus institutional capitulation, but unlikely.

A world where AI agents hold genuine independent economic or political power roughly matching humans is a natural intermediate stage and could emerge if autonomous agents accumulate resources and legal standing quickly. Still less likely than continued human ultimate authority within four years.

The overwhelming default on a four-year horizon is that humans, governments, and firms retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and compute, whether because capabilities stay below transformative thresholds or because control mechanisms keep pace.

An actor establishing a civilization-wide enforcement system that actively prevents structural change requires global monopoly on decisive capability plus surveillance reach that no state or lab will have by 2030. Current multipolar competition between US and Chinese labs makes this remote.

Would require dismantling fabs, compute clusters, and research capacity worldwide and keeping that in force, against overwhelming commercial and military incentives. Even a severe AI-caused disaster would more likely produce regulation than genuine surrender of capability within four years.
Joint extinction of humans and AI by 2030 requires a catastrophic scenario such as nuclear war or runaway replicators, which is very unlikely in this window.
Humanity being gone by 2030 with a value-preserving AI successor is extremely unlikely on this timeline.
Misaligned AI exterminating humanity by 2030 is a real but small tail risk given the short timeline and physical constraints.
A multipolar AI competition with humans marginalized would need rapid loss of human control, which is unlikely by 2030.
Causally separated regions with different states would require space settlement or isolation that is implausible by 2030.
Identity-continuous human-AI integration as the dominant structure by 2030 is highly unlikely.
AI holding decisive power while humans survive is possible only with a rapid takeoff that leaves humans alive.
Humans and AI as roughly equal separate powers is an unstable intermediate that is unlikely to be the state on this date.
Humans most likely retain ultimate authority over AI through 2030, with capabilities either sub-transformative or controlled.
A civilization-wide system actively freezing structural change is unlikely to be established by 2030, though authoritarian AI-enabled control is a tail.
Deliberately dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI is very unlikely given the economic and strategic incentives.
Extinction of both humans and AI by 2030 would require a catastrophe far faster than any credible trajectory. Tail risk from accident or conflict keeps it above zero.
A deliberate handover to AI heirs with humanity wholly gone is not plausible within this window. Its requirements are far beyond anything in view by 2030.
Humanity being displaced by AI pursuing indifferent goals by 2030 is a low-probability tail. It would need rapid capability gains and loss of control that have not yet appeared.
Many competing autonomous AI systems with humanity marginalized would need a fast diffusion of agentic capability and loss of human leverage. This is a tail scenario for 2030.
Causally separated regions would need to diverge into different structural states, which is possible under fragmentation but requires isolation between regions. The overall probability is modest.
Identity-continuous integration of humans and AI becoming dominant by 2030 is far beyond current neurotechnology and biology. Ordinary implants and tool use do not qualify.
AI holding decisive power while humans survive without steering would require a transfer of control that has not yet happened. It is a tail scenario by 2030.

Humans and AI remaining distinct with both holding substantial power is a plausible state if capabilities grow while human institutions keep some leverage. It fits a world of strong but contested AI actors.

Humans most likely retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and resources through 2030, with AI acting autonomously only within delegated bounds. Current institutions, labs, and governments are still exercising this control, and capability growth is unlikely to remove it within four years.
An actor establishing a civilization-wide system that actively freezes the human-AI arrangement would require unusual centralization. This is possible but unlikely within four years.
Deliberate, enforced worldwide abandonment of powerful AI capability would require an extraordinary coordination success that has not been on track. The probability is very low.

AI-enabled catastrophe provides a route to human extinction before machines establish independently sustainable infrastructure. Complete extinction of both humans and AI requires substantially more than economic collapse or mass casualties.

This outcome requires complete human extinction alongside a surviving AI civilization that faithfully preserves human values. The conjunction has no strong near-term pathway, especially because identity-continuous transformation belongs elsewhere.

Rapid capability gains, misaligned objectives, and decisive strategic advantage provide a route to human extinction followed by autonomous AI continuation. Completing both extinction and industrial independence by 2030 imposes demanding physical and temporal constraints.

Competitive deployment and proliferation of autonomous agents create a route to distributed machine power without a single dominant coalition. Qualifying requires humans to lose their position as a roughly equal power, not simply to depend heavily on competing AI services.

Civilization remains concentrated within a tightly connected terrestrial and near-Earth environment. Political fragmentation and communications restrictions do not establish the causal separation required by this category.

Civilization-wide integration requires breakthroughs in identity-continuous interfaces or transformation, followed by extraordinarily rapid adoption. Ordinary AI assistance and limited neural implants leave humans and AI meaningfully distinct.

Control over research, cyber operations, production, and institutional decisions provides a route from delegated autonomy to decisive AI power. Human survival requires neither human sovereignty nor successful alignment with human preferences.

Independent AI agency alongside continued human control of physical resources supports a transitional balance of power. Human institutions, infrastructure ownership, and competing systems create counterweights to unilateral machine dominance.

The strongest base rate is continued human authority through ownership, infrastructure control, deployment decisions, and institutional adaptation. Four years constrains the transition from impressive capabilities to independent civilizational power, and this category includes highly autonomous systems operating under ultimate human authority.

AI-enabled surveillance, coercion, and concentrated technological advantage provide mechanisms for enforcing a fixed civilizational arrangement. Establishing such enforcement across all civilization requires overcoming geopolitical competition and preventing structural challengers, not merely consolidating national authoritarian rule.

Commercial incentives, military competition, and widely distributed technical knowledge oppose civilization-wide surrender of powerful AI capability. Regulation, emergency pauses, and restrictions on deployment do not meet the requirement to dismantle the practical ability to build it.
Rapid capability growth creates pathways to catastrophic conflict and loss of control. Extinction of both humans and AI by 2030 requires an unusually comprehensive disaster.
This outcome requires complete human extinction alongside surviving AI that faithfully carries forward human values. That conjunction occupies less than one probability point over this short horizon.

Misaligned systems gaining strategic superiority provide a direct route to human extinction without continuity. Completing that transition by 2030 requires rapid advances in autonomous research, resource acquisition, and physical execution.
