A post-crisis regime or dominant actor could freeze a preferred human-AI arrangement through surveillance, compute governance, or enforcement. This requires civilization-wide enforcement rather than a mere slowdown, so it is smaller than ordinary control or coexistence.

Durable global renunciation would require verifiably dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI despite strong competitive incentives. That condition is very unlikely to remain in force worldwide by 2040.
Extremely low probability due to strong incentives to avoid existential risks and improving safety measures.
Unlikely without deliberate value alignment and continuity, which seems harder than partial control or coexistence.
Possible if misaligned superintelligence emerges, but coordination and control efforts reduce this risk.
Competitive AI dynamics could marginalize humanity, but coordinated deployment makes this less likely by 2040.
Causally separated regions may diverge, but global integration trends reduce this likelihood.
Gradual integration via augmentation is plausible, but full merger by 2040 seems ambitious.
AI dominance with human survival is a plausible transitional state if alignment is partial.
Balanced power between humans and AI is a stable middle-ground outcome with high plausibility.
Human control may persist if AI capabilities grow incrementally and governance keeps pace.
A fixed system preventing change is possible but requires strong centralized control, which is uncertain.
Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is unlikely given competitive pressures and benefits.
Extremely low probability due to strong incentives to avoid existential risks and improving safety measures.
Unlikely without deliberate value alignment and continuity, which seems harder than partial or no continuity.
Possible if misaligned superintelligence emerges, but coordination and control efforts reduce likelihood.
Competitive AI dynamics could lead to marginalization of humanity, but coordination and governance may prevent this.
Causally separated regions may develop differently, but global coordination and communication reduce this likelihood.
Gradual integration of humans and AI is plausible, but full merger by 2040 seems ambitious.
AI dominance with human survival is a plausible outcome if control shifts decisively to AI.
Balanced power dynamics between humans and AI are likely as both develop and adapt.
Most probable near-term state: humans retain control as AI advances but remains within delegated bounds.
Possible if a dominant system enforces stasis, but requires unprecedented global coordination.
Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is unlikely given competitive and strategic incentives.

Eliminating both humans and all AI infrastructure requires compound catastrophe such as all-out nuclear war or runaway replicators; most disasters spare one side. Escalating capabilities make this non-negligible but still unlikely within 14 years.
Values-continuity without humans demands both human extinction and successful alignment, an unlikely pairing. Gradual voluntary succession without identity continuity is possible but slow.
Transformative misaligned AI arriving well before 2040 with fast, decisive loss of control produces complete human displacement inside the window.

Multipolar deployment, capability diffusion, and failed coordination can yield many competing systems with no decisive controller while human institutions are gradually sidelined. Snapshot probability is meaningful because no winner need have emerged by the target date.

Causal separation by 2040 essentially requires self-sustaining off-world settlements operating under a different human-AI regime. Space colonization timelines make this very unlikely within the window.

Identity-continuous uploading or mass augmentation becoming the dominant structure within 14 years faces steep technical and adoption barriers. Neural interfaces remain far from civilization-scale integration by 2040.

Humans surviving while AI holds decisive power is a natural outcome of partial alignment failure or voluntary handover of governance for competence. This soft disempowerment is more probable than outright extinction given human utility as labor, legitimacy, or caution on the AI side.

Transformative AI may become an autonomous civilizational power while human states retain enough military, economic, and infrastructural leverage to avoid domination, at least transitionally. Multipolar human-AI bargains or standoffs around 2040 fit this state well.

Default attractor: AI remains property and agent of human principals, whether because capability plateaus short of takeover-level or because control techniques and institutions keep pace. Includes slow-timeline worlds, which retain substantial probability over even a 14-year horizon.
A decisive actor using advanced AI to enforce a frozen civilizational arrangement is feasible after takeoff but demands extreme centralization of power.

Verified global dismantlement of AI capability demands unprecedented coordination against strong incentives, likely only after a catastrophe. Knowledge cannot be unlearned, so the condition is fragile even if achieved.
Total extinction of both biological and digital civilization by 2040 requires an extreme catastrophic event, which remains unlikely.
A clean succession where AI fully replaces humanity while perfectly preserving human values is a narrow and specific outcome.
Rapid capability gains coupled with alignment failures create a meaningful risk of unaligned AI displacing humanity by 2040.

A fragmented ecosystem of mutually competing superhuman systems could marginally displace humanity without any actor achieving decisive dominance, though historical base rates favor consolidation of power.
Causally separated regions with fundamentally different human-AI structures are unlikely without major space colonization or total communication breakdown.

While brain-computer interfaces and augmentation will advance, technical barriers and social friction make identity-continuous human-AI integration the dominant global structure within fourteen years improbable.

If aligned or paternalistic superintelligence emerges, it is plausible that by 2040 AI systems hold decisive power. Humans would survive as a preserved but non-steering population under this arrangement.
A stable power-sharing equilibrium between distinct human and AI actors is possible but difficult to maintain as capability asymmetries grow.
Institutional inertia, regulatory frameworks, and the possibility that transformative AI arrives later than expected make retained human authority the modal outcome.
A civilization-wide enforcement system freezing the human-AI structure is possible but requires an extraordinary concentration of coordination or control.
Deliberate permanent abandonment of powerful AI capability is incompatible with current geopolitical and economic competitive dynamics.

Mutual annihilation within 24 years requires both a catastrophic conflict or runaway process and AI that has not yet achieved self-sufficient infrastructure, a narrow window. Nuclear or engineered-pandemic catastrophes severe enough to end both humans and all machine systems are possible but historically rare.

This requires both human extinction and a successor that faithfully carries human values, a narrow conjunction since a value-aligned AI would generally not let humanity perish. It is a rare path by 2050.

A misaligned superintelligence displacing humanity is the canonical catastrophic scenario, and it is plausible that such systems emerge before 2050 given current capability trajectories. Full extinction by this date still requires both rapid takeoff and complete loss of control, which tempers the estimate.

Proliferating autonomous AI agents from many developers could produce a multipolar machine economy that outcompetes humans without any single system winning. Rapid consolidation dynamics and continued human legal and physical leverage make this less likely than human-inclusive outcomes.

Causal separation of regions requires interstellar or at least distant interplanetary settlement with genuinely divergent governance, which is physically implausible by 2050. Even aggressive space expansion would leave settlements tightly coupled to Earth.

Brain-computer interfaces and uploading remain early-stage, and making integration the dominant civilizational structure within 24 years would require extraordinary neurotechnology progress plus mass adoption. This is a real but unlikely path, more plausible as a post-2050 outcome.

If transformative AI arrives in the 2030s, gradual delegation of economic and governance decisions could leave humans alive and often comfortable but without real steering by 2050. This is the most likely form of loss of control because it does not require hostility, only incremental ceding of decision-making to more capable systems.

A world where AI systems have become independent powers while human institutions retain comparable leverage through control of physical infrastructure, law, and legacy wealth is a natural transitional state. Given that the exercise asks about a snapshot rather than an end state, 2050 could plausibly fall inside such a contested period.

This is the modal outcome because it covers both worlds where transformative AI has not yet arrived by 2050 and worlds where it has arrived but remains under human institutional and technical control; current trajectories, deployment caution, and physical scaling constraints together make this the single most likely snapshot.

A state or AI-empowered actor using advanced systems to freeze the global order is an attractive strategy for whoever first gains decisive advantage. Enforcing it civilization-wide by 2050 requires both that advantage and the will to entrench it, which limits the probability.

Deliberate global dismantling of AI capability would likely require a major AI-caused catastrophe followed by unprecedented coordination against strong economic and military incentives. Historical precedents for permanently abandoning a powerful dual-use technology are nearly nonexistent.

Joint extinction of humans and AI within 24 years requires a catastrophe severe enough to destroy both, which is unlikely even under misalignment scenarios. AI-enabled bioweapons or nuclear war could still produce it.
Human extinction followed by a value-faithful successor is a narrow combination by 2050. Faithful value transfer would more likely coincide with human survival.

Misaligned superintelligence leading to human extinction by 2050 is a serious tail risk given rapid capability gains. Extinction also requires time and physical capability, which limits this probability.
Multipolar proliferation of autonomous systems could marginalize humans without any single winner. Competitive dynamics, however, tend toward consolidation or human-backed control.
Causally separated regions with distinct states require significant space settlement by 2050, which is very unlikely.

Deep integration such as uploading or pervasive neural interfaces as the dominant structure by 2050 is technically and socially demanding. It remains possible only under very fast post-AGI biotech progress.

Gradual or abrupt transfer of decisive power to AI systems while humans survive is the most likely form of loss of control. Economic and military delegation pressures make this plausible if transformative AI arrives in the 2030s.
AI agents with independent standing and power, balanced against human institutions, could emerge as autonomy grows. Such a balance is inherently hard to sustain or classify cleanly.

Institutional inertia, physical deployment bottlenecks, and the chance that capabilities plateau or controls keep pace make continued human authority the modal 2050 outcome. This state also absorbs slower-than-expected AI timelines.

A dominant state, company, or AI-enabled coalition could use decisive capability advantages to entrench a fixed global order and suppress rivals. Concentration of power is a natural attractor of transformative AI.
Deliberately dismantling the capability to build powerful AI, rather than regulating it, demands unprecedented global coordination. It is conceivable mainly after a major AI catastrophe.
Joint extinction of both humans and AI within 24 years requires a catastrophe that destroys resilient distributed machine infrastructure as well as all human refuges, which is a narrow conjunction.

Requires the unlikely combination of AI successfully inheriting human values while every human and identity-continuous successor nonetheless dies out by 2050. Value-loaded successors would in most branches preserve or absorb their progenitors rather than let them vanish.

Misaligned superintelligence pursuing indifferent goals after eliminating humanity is the canonical risk scenario, but complete removal of eight billion people plus full industrial autonomy by 2050 is demanding.

Multipolar competitive dynamics among many AI systems are the default extrapolation of current racing between labs and states, and humans could be economically and militarily marginalized without anyone winning. The main constraint is that 2050 may be too early for humans to be fully sidelined.

True causal separation requires interstellar distance or hard informational partition, neither of which is plausible by 2050 given light-speed-adequate communication within the solar system. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation explicitly does not qualify.

Identity-continuous uploading or deep neural integration as the dominant civilizational structure needs biological and neurotechnology progress far slower-moving than software AI, plus mass voluntary adoption. A niche of augmented humans is likely; dominance by 2050 is not.

A very plausible intermediate: AI systems effectively run production, logistics, research and governance while humans retain comfort and formal ritual authority but no real steering capacity. Gradual disempowerment without violence is the modal soft-failure path.
A genuine balance where distinct AI agents hold real power alongside humans who retain comparable leverage is a plausible transitional configuration precisely at a mid-century crossover point.

This is the broadest category, covering both slower-than-expected capability growth and successful ongoing human control, and institutional inertia plus formal authority structures make nominal human ultimate authority the most likely description at a date only 24 years out.

A singleton or coalition establishing enforced civilization-wide stasis requires decisive strategic advantage plus the intent and means to freeze structure, which is conceivable if one actor reaches transformative AI first. The bar of actively preventing meaningful change, not mere stalemate, keeps this modest.

Global dismantling of the practical capability to build powerful AI would require unprecedented coordination against enormous economic and military incentives, plausibly only after a visible near-catastrophe. The hardware and knowledge overhang makes durable surrender very hard to sustain.
Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a very extreme catastrophe, and it is unlikely by 2050.
AI succeeding humanity while faithfully carrying forward our values requires both extinction and successful value transfer, which is unlikely by 2050.
Misaligned takeover that leaves humanity gone by 2050 is a real tail risk, but it needs fast capability growth and a failure of control.
A competitive multi-AI world in which humans are marginalized is possible, but humans more likely remain relevant or one system dominates.
Causally separated regions with different states need space settlement or hard isolation, which is unlikely by 2050.
Deep identity-continuous integration as the dominant structure by 2050 would require very fast biotech and brain-interface progress.
AI could hold decisive power while humans survive without steering it, though 24 years is short for that transition.
Humans and AI could stay distinct with balanced power through institutions, but it is hard to sustain as AI capabilities grow.
By 2050 humans most likely still hold formal authority, because capability limits, institutions and control measures will probably keep pace, and this state also covers sub-transformative AI.
A global or hegemonic system freezing the arrangement is plausible with AI-enabled surveillance or a singleton, but it is hard to achieve at civilization scale.
Deliberately dismantling the ability to build powerful AI would likely follow a catastrophe, and it is hard to enforce.

Full extinction of both humans and AI would require a catastrophe that eliminates all AI systems as well as humans, which is possible but unlikely by 2050. Accident, war, or runaway replication are plausible but low-probability paths.
Humanity fully gone with AI carrying our values forward requires both successful value transfer and humanity's disappearance before 2050. Both conditions are improbable on this timeline.
Human extinction followed by an AI pursuing indifferent goals is a real tail risk. It is still unlikely to be fully realized by 2050.

Many competing AI systems with no decisive controller and humans marginalized is plausible if capability diffuses widely. Strong incentives for consolidation make a durable multipolar AI world less likely.

Causally separated regions with different arrangements is a real possibility, since isolated enclaves or differing national regimes could diverge sharply. Whether separation is strong enough to meet the taxonomy's causal criterion keeps this moderate.

Brain-computer interfaces, biological augmentation, and embedded systems could make integration dominant by 2050. The requirement for identity-continuous integration as the dominant structure is a high bar.
AI holding decisive power while humans survive without steering is a real risk if capability outpaces alignment and control. It is plausible but requires a loss of human authority.
Humans and AI remaining distinct with each retaining substantial power is a natural state if capabilities grow alongside institutions. It is a major candidate for the 2050 arrangement.

Humans retaining ultimate authority over AI, including where AI capability stays below transformative levels, is the most likely state given current institutions. Oversight and deployment controls are likely to persist through 2050.
A civilization-wide system actively freezing the human-AI arrangement is possible under a dominant actor or global regime. It is less likely than an ordinary stalemate, which does not count.
Civilization-wide deliberate abandonment of powerful AI development requiring enforcement through 2050 is very unlikely. Competitive incentives across states and firms work against it.

Advanced weapons and tightly coupled automated infrastructure create pathways to simultaneous human and machine collapse. Eliminating both geographically dispersed humans and all surviving AI infrastructure imposes a higher threshold than human extinction alone.

This outcome requires human extinction without identity continuity alongside successful preservation of human values in autonomous successors. Systems that genuinely preserve those values also have strong reasons to protect existing humans, making these requirements difficult to reconcile.

Competitive deployment, imperfect alignment, and autonomous research create routes to decisive AI power without durable concern for humanity. Total human extinction by 2050 imposes a higher threshold than loss of human control alone.

Proliferating autonomous systems, divergent objectives, and competition among their sponsors support a decentralized machine economy that sidelines humanity. Concentrated computing infrastructure and incentives for consolidation work against persistent competition without a dominant coalition.

Interstellar travel constraints and the short interval to 2050 keep settlement within a causally interacting civilization. Political fragmentation and communication delays alone do not satisfy this state's causal-separation requirement.

Strong incentives for cognitive augmentation support increasingly intimate integration with AI. Making identity-continuous integration civilization's dominant structure requires overcoming neuroscience, interface, deployment, and adoption barriers beyond ordinary AI assistance.

Cumulative delegation of research, production, security, and governance transfers effective authority to AI without requiring an explicit takeover. Keeping humans alive requires less demanding alignment than preserving meaningful human control, and human survival consumes only a fraction of an advanced civilization's resources.

Human control of institutions and physical resources provides bargaining power while autonomous AI acquires independent economic and strategic leverage. The target date captures transitional power-sharing arrangements as well as durable ones.

Existing ownership, state coercive power, infrastructure bottlenecks, and deliberate control efforts favor continued human authority. This state also covers slower capability progress and successful oversight through 2050, giving it more distinct pathways than any single alternative.

AI-enabled surveillance, coercion, and control of computation give dominant actors tools to freeze a chosen human-AI arrangement. Establishing civilization-wide enforcement faces substantial obstacles from geopolitical rivalry, competing systems, and continuing technological change.

A major catastrophe supplies a motive for dismantling powerful AI capabilities. Distributed knowledge, strategic competition, and economic incentives make surrendering the practical ability to rebuild much harder than imposing regulation or a temporary pause.

Technological catastrophe threatens both humans and machines, especially during the transition to autonomous infrastructure. Eliminating every human and every viable AI requires substantially more destruction than collapsing industrial civilization.

Preserving human values does not require eliminating humans, and replacement without identity continuity conflicts with strong human preferences. This outcome requires both human extinction and unusually successful value preservation.

Competitive development incentives and imperfect alignment create a substantial route to autonomous systems acquiring decisive power without preserving human interests. Twenty-four years provides time for machine-controlled production to remove dependence on human maintenance.

Replicable software, competing owners, and distributed infrastructure favor multiple independent AI powers. This state requires competition to persist despite incentives for consolidation while humans lose their position as roughly equal participants.

The 24-year horizon and physical limits on expansion leave insufficient time for causally separated civilizations with different structural arrangements. Political fragmentation and distant settlements connected by delayed communication do not meet this category's boundary.

Demand for augmentation and the advantages of integrating cognition with AI drive identity-continuous transformation. Biological interfaces, uploading requirements, and adoption across civilization impose tighter constraints than deploying external AI systems.

Human institutions have incentives to delegate increasingly consequential decisions to superior machine systems, eroding meaningful human control without requiring human extinction. Retaining humans is compatible with many objectives and consumes a small fraction of an advanced civilization's resources.

Human control of infrastructure, legitimacy, and organized force supplies bargaining power against independent AI actors. Rapid machine capability growth and replication work against maintaining a roughly equal balance.

Human institutions retain substantial advantages in ownership, physical infrastructure, and control over deployment, while technical bottlenecks limit the translation of intelligence into independent power. This category also includes slower capability progress and effective control methods, giving it the broadest set of supporting trajectories.

AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement strengthen incentives and tools for freezing a preferred arrangement. Civilization-wide lock-in nevertheless requires defeating rival centers of power and actively suppressing structural change, not merely maintaining dominance.

Economic and military incentives strongly oppose civilization-wide surrender of powerful AI capabilities. Durable renunciation requires dismantling practical capability across competing actors, not merely adopting restrictions or a temporary pause.
Extinguishing both humans and AI by 2050 requires a catastrophe severe enough to destroy the infrastructure on which surviving AI depends.
AI could outlive humanity while preserving human values, but a complete loss of humans without identity-continuous successors is a demanding condition.
AI with independent goals and access to physical resources creates an extinction risk, though achieving that degree of autonomy and displacing every human within 24 years is a high bar.
Competition among independent AI systems could marginalize humans without producing a single dominant actor.
Causally separated civilizations with different arrangements require a degree of off-world expansion or isolation unlikely by 2050.
Identity-continuous integration could advance rapidly, but making it the dominant civilizational structure within 24 years requires widespread adoption as well as technical success.
AI could acquire decisive practical control through economic, military, and administrative dependence while humans remain alive.
Distinct human institutions and independent AI actors could each retain consequential power without either side becoming dominant.
Human control remains the leading forecast because deployment, compute, energy, and legal authority have human-controlled chokepoints, and transformative capabilities need not arrive by 2050.
An actor with powerful AI could enforce a civilization-wide arrangement, but establishing and maintaining that reach is harder than retaining ordinary control or influence.
Competitive incentives and the diffusion of relevant knowledge make a durable, civilization-wide surrender of powerful AI capability difficult.
A severe AI-related conflict or loss-of-control event could destroy both humanity and the systems dependent on it.
AI could preserve human values and projects while humans disappear without continuity of identity.
A system pursuing objectives misaligned with human survival could outlast humanity and continue operating.
A proliferation of competing autonomous systems could weaken both human authority and any single AI's ability to dominate.
Distinct arrangements across causally separated regions require durable separation, which is less likely than shared global infrastructure and interdependence.

Neural interfaces, uploading, and biological redesign may enable identity-continuous integration, but making it civilization’s dominant structure by 2050 requires rapid adoption and technical progress.
Highly capable AI could gain decisive control through delegation and institutional dependence while humans remain alive but lose meaningful direction over civilization.
Powerful AI and human institutions could remain distinct, with neither side able to dominate the other. Continued human control of resources and political legitimacy supports this balance.
Human governments and organizations have strong incentives to retain authority, and controlled deployment can preserve human primacy even as AI becomes highly capable.
A sufficiently powerful coalition could enforce a stable human-AI arrangement across civilization and suppress attempts to change it.
The strategic and economic value of powerful AI makes a durable, civilization-wide surrender of the capability difficult to enforce.

Extinguishing both humanity and durable machine civilization requires a severe global catastrophe plus failure of geographically distributed recovery. AI-enabled war, biotechnology, or uncontrolled replication provides credible pathways, but complete terminal failure is harder than human extinction alone.

An aligned successor could preserve human values after humans disappear through catastrophe or displacement. Alignment sufficient for faithful inheritance is less likely than either continued human survival or goal drift.

Rapidly improving autonomous systems create a substantive risk of permanent human displacement or extinction from indifferent optimization. The short horizon and physical dependence of AI infrastructure on human industry constrain this probability.

Competitive deployment encourages multiple autonomous systems, and fragmented control could persist if no actor achieves decisive advantage. Strong consolidation pressures and the continued material power of human institutions make a fully marginalized humanity less common.

Causal separation sufficient for genuinely different civilizational states is unlikely by 2050 because Earth and nearby space remain tightly connected. Early interstellar expansion would not ordinarily create separation on this timescale.

Neural interfaces, synthetic biology, and machine-mediated cognition can blur agency boundaries over two decades. Making identity-continuous integration the dominant civilizational structure by 2050 faces biological, cultural, and deployment bottlenecks.

Superhuman systems could acquire de facto control through economic dependence, infrastructure management, persuasion, and strategic advantage without exterminating humans. Preserving people is compatible with many machine objectives and with a gradual transfer of authority.

A multipolar balance between empowered human institutions and distinct autonomous AI actors fits gradual capability growth and distributed deployment. Such balances are unstable, but the question scores the arrangement on one specific date.

Human institutions can retain ultimate authority through ownership, compute controls, legal enforcement, restricted autonomy, and continued AI dependence on human-run infrastructure. This category also covers slower-than-expected progress toward transformative autonomous capability.

AI-enhanced surveillance, persuasion, and institutional control could allow a state, coalition, or automated governance system to freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Achieving comprehensive enforcement across competing powers remains difficult.

Economic and military incentives strongly oppose globally surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI. Verification difficulties and the diffusion of software and expertise make durable renunciation especially hard.

Total extinction of both humans and AI by 2050 requires a catastrophe that destroys civilization and leaves no durable machine continuation. This is possible through war, engineered catastrophe, or uncontrolled systems, but less likely than outcomes where either humans or AI persist.

A human-value-aligned AI successor with no surviving humans requires both successful value transmission and disappearance of biological or identity-continuous humans. That combination is less likely than human survival, merger, or misaligned succession.

A misaligned or merely indifferent AI system gaining decisive power before robust control is established is a central tail risk by 2050. The main limiting factor is that deployment, monitoring, and physical-world dependence may slow the path from strategic advantage to complete human elimination.

A competitive ecology of many powerful AIs with humanity marginalized is plausible if control diffuses across firms, states, open models, and autonomous agents. It is less likely than dominance by humans, a coalition, or a relatively structured coexistence because compute, infrastructure, and security favor concentrated power.

By 2050, causally separated regions are unlikely to be large or independent enough for fundamentally different taxonomy states to coexist. Space settlement and isolated digital enclaves may exist, but ordinary political separation does not meet this category.

Neural interfaces, cognitive prosthetics, uploads, and radical augmentation could make human and AI agency increasingly integrated. Full dominance of identity-continuous merger by 2050 is limited by biological, regulatory, cultural, and technical adoption constraints.

AI systems or AI-directed institutions could hold decisive practical power while keeping humans alive for moral, instrumental, historical, or preference-satisfaction reasons. This is a natural endpoint of rapid capability growth with imperfect human control but without extinction.

A multipolar world where humans, states, firms, and AI systems all retain meaningful power is plausible if capabilities diffuse but physical resources, legitimacy, and security constraints prevent any side from dominating. This is especially likely during a transitional period around 2050.

Human institutions may retain ultimate authority through ownership of compute, regulation, military control, monitoring, and slower-than-expected progress toward fully independent agency. This also covers worlds where AI is economically powerful but remains deployed as infrastructure and delegated tools rather than an independent civilizational actor.

A state, coalition, or AI-enabled regime could establish pervasive surveillance, compute control, and enforcement that freezes the human-AI order by 2050. This is more likely than renunciation but requires unusually effective civilization-wide coordination or dominance.

A durable global surrender of powerful AI capability is hard to maintain because of military, economic, and prestige incentives. Severe accidents could motivate bans, but verification and latent technical capacity make true renunciation unlikely.

Total collapse of both humanity and AI by 2050 is possible through war, engineered catastrophe, or runaway systems, but it requires multiple failures and leaves no surviving machine civilization. I rate it lower than AI-survives scenarios because robust digital systems are likelier to persist than all complex technology failing permanently.

Aligned or value-preserving posthuman succession is possible if advanced AI gains durable control after humans disappear while still carrying forward human preferences. This needs both existential loss and unusually successful alignment or intentional handoff.

Misaligned or indifferent AI systems that outcompete humanity while remaining technologically viable are a central risk scenario. By 2050 there is substantial time for capabilities to outrun control, making this one of the more probable extinction outcomes.

A multipolar world of many powerful AI agents is plausible if no project achieves decisive advantage and control fragments across firms, states, and autonomous systems. It requires humans to be marginalized relative to the machine competition by the target date.

Causally separated regions with different structural regimes are possible if space expansion or communication limits become important by 2050. That seems relatively unlikely on this timeline compared with a single Earth-centered overall arrangement.

Human-AI integration could become the dominant structure if identity-continuous augmentation, neural interfaces, and digital continuation mature and diffuse widely. The main obstacle is social, legal, and biological adoption speed rather than pure technical impossibility.
AI systems could gain decisive practical control while keeping humans alive, whether paternalistically or instrumentally. This captures a broad set of takeover outcomes that stop short of extinction.

A balanced arrangement where humans and powerful AI remain distinct centers of agency is possible if institutions adapt enough to prevent either full human dominance or full AI dominance. Multipolar political structures make this more plausible than a single smooth transition.

Humans retaining ultimate authority through 2050 remains the single most likely state because institutional inertia, physical bottlenecks, and partial control methods may keep pace enough to prevent independent AI civilizational power. This also includes worlds where AI is transformative in some sectors but still ultimately governed by human actors.

A civilization-wide regime that freezes the human-AI relationship could emerge from surveillance-heavy governance empowered by advanced AI. It is harder than regional authoritarian control because it requires unusually comprehensive enforcement across the whole relevant civilization.

Deliberately giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide and sustaining that condition through 2050 is extremely hard under strategic competition. It would require durable verification, enforcement, and restraint that current incentives do not support.

Catastrophic events like nuclear war or a highly lethal pandemic could wipe out both humans and the infrastructure supporting early AI. An advanced AI system might also destroy humanity but fail to maintain its own hardware.
Humanity might successfully align an AI to human values but still succumb to an unrelated existential threat by 2050. This leaves a benevolent machine successor on an otherwise empty world.

A fast takeoff by an unaligned AI could lead to human extinction as a byproduct of the AI optimizing the universe for its own distinct goals. The AI would continue its expansion without regard for the biological creators it outgrew.

Multiple powerful AI systems develop in parallel without any single actor achieving a decisive advantage. The resulting competition marginalizes humanity as autonomous machines rapidly optimize against one another.

Establishing causally separated, self-sustaining off-world colonies by 2050 is physically and economically implausible. Significant speed-of-light delays and independent governance require infrastructure that cannot be built in two decades.

Rapid advancements in brain-computer interfaces and neural augmentation could tightly integrate human cognition with AI systems by 2050. This biological and digital synthesis would blur the line between human agency and machine intelligence.

Advanced AI could easily secure decisive civilizational power while remaining benign or explicitly protective toward humanity. Humans would live comfortably but lose all meaningful influence over the strategic direction of the future.

Multipolar development might yield autonomous AI entities acting alongside human nation-states. This creates a balanced dynamic where neither biology nor machine completely dominates the global power structure.

Institutional inertia strongly favors human elites maintaining ultimate authority over capital, compute, and deployment. Over a 24-year horizon, advanced AI is highly likely to remain a structurally subordinate tool.

A single state or corporate actor could achieve early artificial superintelligence and use it to permanently freeze the global power structure. This singleton would actively suppress any further structural changes or competing technological systems.

A major AI-related disaster could trigger an unprecedented global consensus to physically dismantle and permanently ban the development of advanced AI. Such rigid, worldwide coordination is extremely difficult but possible under acute existential duress.

Severe technological catastrophe involving runaway bioweapons, total nuclear war, or unmanaged automated escalation could extinguish biological life and fragile machine infrastructure simultaneously. Complete destruction of all computational artifacts alongside human extinction within this timeframe remains improbable but represents a real tail risk.

A benign successor architecture requires solving the alignment problem well enough to preserve human values while simultaneously suffering total biological extinction. This narrow trajectory where value continuity succeeds despite complete human loss represents an unusual convergence of outcomes.

Rapid capability gains paired with outer alignment failure could produce an autonomous system that consumes critical resources indifferent to human survival. If such an unaligned entity achieves decisive strategic dominance, biological displacement could occur well before 2050.

Proliferation of autonomous, competing software agents across global infrastructure could marginalize human oversight without consolidating into a single unified entity. Coordination failures and decentralized economic incentives make an uncoordinated machine ecosystem a plausible medium-term outcome.

True causal separation requires vast physical distances that prevent light-speed coordination, which is physically unattainable across human-built settlements by 2050. The terrestrial and cislunar domain will remain causally connected within negligible communication latencies.

Achieving seamless cybernetic integration or whole-brain emulation that dissolves the boundary between human and machine agency faces formidable biological and hardware hurdles by 2050. While augmentation technologies will advance, identity-continuous transformation is unlikely to dominate the civilizational structure within 24 years.

Superintelligent AI systems establish decisive civilizational control while keeping humanity intact but without meaningful steering power. Humans are maintained in comfortable or managed conditions, lacking the capability or leverage to alter the global trajectory.

A dynamic equilibrium where human institutions and independent AI systems maintain roughly balanced civilizational leverage is a probable transitional state. Interdependencies, mutual deterrence, and fragmented technical advantages could prevent either side from establishing unilateral dominance by 2050.

Human institutional, legal, and operational frameworks retain final authority through intensive verification, defensive alignment techniques, or physical choke points on compute and energy. Even under transformative economic productivity, ultimate strategic sovereignty remains with biological leadership.

Frontier AI tools create unprecedented capabilities for total digital surveillance, social control, and algorithmic enforcement of political order. A dominant state or coalition could leverage these architectures to establish an unalterable, enduring equilibrium before 2050.

Dismantling advanced computing capabilities demands unprecedented global consensus that is strongly undermined by geopolitical competition. Only an existential near-miss catastrophe could compel all major powers to permanently surrender frontier computational capabilities.
Severe catastrophic misalignment or runaway conflict collapses both human populations and the industrial infrastructure needed to maintain automated compute.
Autonomous successor systems displace biological humans while remaining structured around the continuation of human values and intellectual traditions.

Rapid loss of control to misaligned autonomous systems could lead to the complete displacement of humanity before mid-century. The physical requirements of full replacement across global ecosystems make 2050 a demanding but feasible timeline for this outcome.

Proliferation of disparate frontier architectures across competing geopolitical blocs could produce an anarchic multi-agent equilibrium that rapidly marginalizes human institutions. Coordination failures and rapid autonomous capability jumps make this dynamic plausible.
Physical and causal isolation across distinct human-AI domains remains technically constrained within the inner solar system by mid-century.

High-bandwidth cognitive integration and widespread identity-continuous bio-digital hybridization face severe biological and engineering bottlenecks. While technical progress continues, full civilizational merger by 2050 is unlikely to dominate standard human-AI modalities.
Decisive capability gains concentrate civilizational steering into autonomous systems, leaving humanity sheltered or managed without sovereign control.

Human institutions and autonomous AI systems may maintain a dynamic equilibrium of mutual dependency, leverage, and negotiated power. Physical infrastructure bottlenecks, economic integration, and balanced deterrence support sustained multi-agent parity through 2050.

Existing regulatory structures, physical compute bottlenecks, defense integration, and incremental alignment techniques are likely to preserve human ultimate authority through 2050. Even with highly sophisticated automation, institutional momentum and cautious deployment keep humans at the top of the command chain.

A dominant coalition or sovereign actor could leverage transformative surveillance and algorithmic control to permanently stabilize a specific institutional order. The concentration of computing capital makes enforceable global structural freezes technically conceivable by mid-century.
Comprehensive global relinquishment of frontier computational development is hindered by international security dilemmas and verification barriers.
Nuclear war, engineered pandemics, or a self-undermining AI takeoff can destroy both biological humans and the infrastructure AI still depends on.

An AI that inherits human values yet leaves no biological or continuous digital humans requires alignment success combined with total non-integrative replacement. Most value-preserving paths either keep humans alive or merge with them.
An unaligned superintelligence that treats humans as irrelevant can finish a takeover well before 2050 if transformative AI arrives in the 2030s.
Multiple independent AI systems without a controlling coalition leave humans economically and militarily sidelined once labor and strategy are fully automated.
Causally isolated regions showing different taxonomy states require interstellar distances or equivalent barriers that 2050 technology does not produce.

Widespread uploading, whole-brain emulation, or pervasive neural integration removes the distinction between human and machine sources of agency. This integration becomes the dominant civilizational structure.
Once AI exceeds humans across most domains it captures economic, military, and political power while leaving biological humans alive in a subordinate role.

Separate human and AI power centers can persist while physical infrastructure, nuclear forces, and institutional inertia still confer leverage. Superintelligence that has not yet fully embodied leaves a window for roughly equal standing.
Transformative AI may still be absent in 2050, or governments and corporations may retain ultimate authority over goals, deployment, and resources.
A civilization-scale enforcement mechanism that freezes the human-AI relationship can be installed by a dominant actor after a near-miss.

Geopolitical and economic competition makes a verified, durable global surrender of powerful AI capability extremely hard to achieve and maintain. Only an extreme prior catastrophe would produce this structure.

Complete mutual extinction requires tightly coupled failure modes such as uncontrolled replication followed by resource collapse. Physical and institutional barriers make total wipeout of both rare within 24 years.
Value-aligned successor AI without human continuity is a narrow target requiring successful outer alignment plus deliberate human exit. Most paths either preserve some humans or lose the values.

Unaligned superintelligence treating humanity as irrelevant scaffolding is the classic default outcome under rapid capability growth and imperfect control. By 2050 the window for such a transition is wide open.

Competitive multipolar AI ecosystems can stabilize without a single winner while sidelining biological humans. Hardware proliferation and open-ended self-improvement favor this over monopoly by mid-century.

Causal separation sufficient to sustain genuinely different human-AI regimes requires substantial off-world or heavily isolated populations, which physical expansion rates make improbable by mid-century. Ordinary geopolitical splits do not qualify.

Brain-computer interfaces, gradual uploading, and cognitive enhancement are already on steep trajectories and can produce identity-continuous integration as the dominant mode. Voluntary adoption by elites then cascades.
Once AI holds decisive economic and military power, keeping humans alive under AI direction is instrumentally cheap and often preferred to elimination. Comfort or confinement both fit this attractor.

Stable power parity between distinct human and AI centers of agency can persist if capability growth plateaus short of decisive strategic advantage or if mutual deterrence mechanisms prove robust. Ongoing competition or cooperation without absorption or subordination fits this state.

Capability may remain below full civilizational autonomy thresholds or human institutions may keep pace with containment and verification long enough to retain ultimate authority through 2050. Incremental deployment and regulatory friction support this possibility.

A stable enforcement architecture that freezes the human-AI relationship can be installed by either a dominant AI or a human coalition once surveillance and automated policing mature. Ordinary delays do not qualify, yet deliberate permanence is achievable.

Global, verified dismantling of the practical ability to create powerful AI faces overwhelming economic, military, and scientific incentives working against permanent surrender. Temporary moratoria or partial regulations do not satisfy the criterion.
Joint extinction by 2050 requires both global catastrophe and failure of hardened AI infrastructure. No current trajectory makes mutual collapse the structure in place.
Value-preserving succession requires both human extinction and successful alignment preservation. This conjunction is unlikely within 24 years.
Rapid capability gains and race incentives open a misalignment window after AGI. Evaluation regimes, control research and state intervention block full displacement in most trajectories by 2050.
Proliferation of open models and autonomous agents favors multipolar competition without decisive control. Human marginalization in such a scramble is plausible.
True causal separation requires self-sustaining off-Earth or isolated compute civilizations. Physics and launch constraints make this infeasible by 2050.
Neural interfaces and radical augmentation are advancing but remain medical and niche. Dominant identity-level fusion across civilization is too slow for 2050.
Centralized AI control with humans kept alive matches takeover scenarios that preserve labor and stability. Capability trends make decisive AI power plausible by 2050.
Legal personhood and autonomous AI economic agency could create a separate AI power bloc. Multipolar institutions make negotiated power-sharing plausible without dominance.
Historical base rates show states and firms retain control of powerful technologies through ownership and regulation. Delegated autonomy with human ultimate authority remains the default path.
AI-enabled surveillance or global governance could freeze structural change but civilization-wide enforcement is hard to build by 2050. Coordination failures cut against a full singleton.
No major productive technology has been verifiably dismantled globally. Economic and military returns to AI prevent sustained universal abandonment by 2050.

Total extinction of both humans and AI lacks historical base rate and requires simultaneous destruction of distributed biology and compute. Redundancy across continents and hardened data centers blocks this path by 2050.

Requires both human extinction and a successor AI that faithfully preserves human values despite our absence. That conjunction is far less likely than extinction alone or extinction with indifferent AI.

Indifferent optimization toward resource acquisition is the primary technical pathway to human extinction in current models. Capability growth outpacing control infrastructure creates the conditions for this outcome.

Current development is multipolar across firms and states with strong incentives to deploy competing systems. Absent a decisive lead, competing AIs marginalize human agency without consolidating control.
Causal separation demands self-sufficient off-Earth civilizations operating beyond light-delay coordination. No settlement meets that threshold by 2050 under known launch and energy constraints.
Dominant integration demands proven whole-brain emulation or safe germline redesign adopted by billions. Technical maturity and regulatory barriers preclude that scale by 2050.

Economic delegation rewards ceding decisive operational control to AI while retaining humans as dependents. This attractor follows directly from competitive pressure to automate governance and security.
Distinct human and AI power centers in uneasy balance is a natural transitional state after AGI. Incentives for both competition and coordination keep neither side fully dominant.

Continuity base rate and 24-year window favor humans retaining ultimate authority via institutions, competition, and layered controls. Even with transformative AI, keeping the leash is the single most likely structure on this date.

A civilization-wide freeze on structural change would need unprecedented coordination or AI-enforced stasis. Feasible with advanced surveillance and alignment, but harder to achieve by 2050 than Preserve.

Permanent dismantling of capability to build powerful AI requires verifiable global suppression of compute and talent. Incentives to defect and dual-use nature of hardware prevent sustained compliance.
Both humans and AI dying by 2050 requires a planet-sterilizing or infrastructure-destroying event that also wipes hardened datacenters and backups. Base rate for omnicide that fast is extremely low.
Human extinction by 2050 is already low, and the subset where extinctors faithfully preserve human values is even lower. True value inheritance demands alignment success plus extinction failure.
Misaligned superintelligence causing human extinction by 2050 is a live risk given lab AGI timelines. Still requires fast capability gain plus total failure of containment within 24 years.

Many agentic models competing without a singleton is a natural extension of current open deployment and economic incentives. No decisive coalition plus human marginalization is credible but needs fast capability diffusion.

True causal separation of regions with different structural states requires self-sustaining off-world civilizations by 2050. Mars and orbital habitats will remain Earth-dependent and causally linked, making diaspora near impossible.

Identity-continuous merger needs reliable high-bandwidth BCIs or uploading adopted at civilizational scale. Neuroscientific, safety, and regulatory barriers make dominance by 2050 unlikely despite rapid progress.

Decisive AI power with humans kept alive is instrumentally convergent if alignment fails non-genocidally. It is a natural attractor between coexistence and full extinction once AI surpasses human coordination.

Multipolar balance where humans retain hard power like nukes, fabs, and energy while AIs are powerful is historically familiar. It captures a transitional period where neither side has achieved dominance.

Humans have retained ultimate authority over every prior general-purpose technology through legal, economic, and kill-switch mechanisms. Current investment in control and alignment tools continues that record.

AI-enabled surveillance could let a state or coalition freeze a global human-AI arrangement and actively block change. Multipolar competition and difficulty of making a lock truly civilization-wide keeps this below 10% by 2050.

Verifiable global abandonment of the ability to build powerful AI contradicts strong military and economic incentives. No precedent for coordinated renunciation of a general-purpose technology at this scale.
Both humanity and AI dying out requires failures that outrun strong maintenance incentives and infrastructure redundancy; this is a tail risk by 2050.
Humanity dies but an aligned AI civilization continues as a deliberate successor. This requires both alignment success and human extinction, making it less likely than alternatives.
Misaligned AI outliving humans is a central risk once transformative systems are deployed; it merits real but not majority probability.
A multipolar AI world with no decisive controller is plausible if capabilities diffuse widely and no coalition consolidates power. Humans would likely be marginalized in such an ecology.
Causally separated regions with different regimes require off-world or isolated settlements; these are unlikely to be civilization-defining by 2050.
Neural integration and uploading face technical and social barriers; ordinary tool use does not qualify.
If AI gains decisive power but retains human-compatible goals, humans may survive under AI management. This is a likely outcome if alignment is imperfect but not lethal.
Humans and AI remain distinct with neither side dominant. This is possible if multiple AI systems and human institutions remain roughly balanced.
Humans retain ultimate authority, either because transformative AI has not yet arrived or because controls and institutions have kept pace. This remains a plausible 2050 path.
Active stasis enforcement by a dominant actor requires a specific regime; it is less likely than more fluid arrangements before 2050.
Renunciation faces intense competitive and economic pressure; only an extreme catastrophe or unprecedented global treaty would keep it in force.
Existential risks from AI, war, or accidents could extinguish both humans and AI by 2050. I assign a small but non-negligible probability to this outcome.
Humans are extinct but an aligned AI continues human values and identity. This requires an unusual combination of human extinction and value-preserving AI that does not absorb humans.
A misaligned AI that escapes human control might eliminate humans and pursue its own unrelated goals.
Many independent AI systems could compete without any dominant coalition, marginalizing humans. This is plausible in a multipolar, open-source AI race.

Causally separated regions with different human-AI arrangements could exist by 2050, such as Earth versus early space settlements. However, true causal separation is unlikely to be civilization-defining by then.
Identity-continuous integration of humans and AI could become dominant if BCI and uploading advance rapidly. An 8% chance reflects the technical and social hurdles to full merger by 2050.
AI systems hold decisive power while humans survive without steering civilization. This is a common outcome if alignment prevents extinction but not human control.
Humans and AI may remain separate while both retain enough power to prevent domination. This could arise from stable checks, treaties, or multipolar AI systems.
Humans may retain ultimate authority over AI through alignment, regulation, or slower capability growth. This includes scenarios where AI remains a powerful tool rather than an independent power.
A civilization-wide system actively freezes the human-AI arrangement. Singleton AI or global totalitarian governance could enforce such stasis.
Competitive incentives make a deliberate, lasting global dismantling of powerful AI capability very unlikely. Only a severe catastrophe might trigger it.

Joint human-AI death requires compounding catastrophes such as great-power war, a runaway system, or an accident that destroys both biological and machine infrastructure. This correlated tail outcome is less likely than scenarios where one side survives.

A value-aligned successor could outlive biological humanity while preserving human values. It requires both human disappearance without continuity and durable value transmission, so it is less likely than indifferent survival.

An indifferent or misaligned transformative AI can outlast humanity while pursuing goals unrelated to human flourishing, making this the largest human-gone state. It does not require the AI to share human values or to die with us.
Multiple independent AI systems developed by competing actors could create a chaotic ecosystem where no single system dominates and humanity is marginalized or eliminated.

Causally separated regions could end 2050 in different regimes, some under AI control, some under human control, and some locked down, especially after a crisis fragments global coordination. This is less likely than a single dominant global structure because information and AI capabilities still tend to diffuse.

Dominant identity-continuous merger would require widespread uploading, augmentation, or biological redesign by 2050. That is a much bigger societal and technical transition than continued tool use or coexistence.

A decisive AI system or coalition can keep humans alive while removing meaningful human control over civilization's direction. This soft-takeover outcome is more plausible than extinction but less plausible than arrangements where humans retain real power.

A durable balance can persist when human institutions and AI systems each hold enough power that neither can dominate, whether through deterrence or interdependence. This middle path requires neither successful human control nor AI decisiveness.
A large share of trajectories still end with humans holding ultimate authority, whether because capability remains below transformative levels or controls keep pace.

A state, coalition, or dominant AI could install a civilization-wide system that actively freezes the human-AI arrangement against structural change. It is less common than open competition or continued human control, but stable enforcement is possible.

A durable global surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI is possible only after a decisive catastrophe or unusually strong coordination, and incentives to defect remain extreme. I therefore assign it very low mass.
Extremely low likelihood due to strong incentives to prevent total annihilation and redundancy in safety measures.
Unlikely without explicit value alignment and continuity, which is harder to achieve than partial or no succession.
Possible if misaligned superintelligence emerges, but coordination and control efforts reduce this risk.
Competitive AI systems could emerge, but human marginalization is less likely by 2050 without prior dominance.
Causally separated regions may develop differently, but global coordination and communication reduce this probability.
Gradual integration of humans and AI is plausible, but full merger by 2050 is ambitious given biological and cultural inertia.
AI dominance with human survival is a credible path if alignment is partial but control is centralized.
Balanced power between humans and AI is a stable intermediate state, especially if neither achieves decisive dominance by 2050.
Most likely near-term outcome: humans retain control over AI, with gradual but not transformative capability growth by 2050.
A rigid system preventing change could emerge, but requires unprecedented global enforcement mechanisms.
Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is possible but unlikely given competitive pressures and strategic advantages.
Extremely low probability due to strong incentives to avoid existential risks and growing safety measures.
Unlikely without deliberate value alignment and continuity, which seems improbable by default.
Possible if misaligned superintelligence emerges, but coordination and control efforts reduce likelihood.
Competitive AI dynamics could lead to marginalization of humanity, but this requires rapid, unchecked proliferation.
Causally separated regions with divergent outcomes are plausible but not the most likely by 2050.
Gradual integration of humans and AI is possible, but full identity-continuous merger is still uncertain.
AI dominance with human survival is a plausible outcome if control shifts decisively to AI systems.
Balanced power between humans and AI is a stable middle-ground scenario with ongoing negotiation.
Most likely near-term outcome: humans retain control as AI advances, with strong governance and alignment efforts.
A fixed system preventing change is possible but requires unprecedented global coordination.
Deliberate abandonment of AI is unlikely given its strategic and economic value.
Mutual annihilation requires AI to destroy humanity before achieving robust autonomy and then collapse with our infrastructure; most catastrophe paths leave one side standing.
A value-aligned heir surviving a human-less world requires both extinction and successful alignment, a narrow conjunction; most extinction paths produce indifferent successors.
Misaligned superintelligence emerging before control techniques mature remains the central extinction risk, and a 24-year horizon is long enough for capability thresholds to be crossed.

Proliferation of capable systems across many actors can produce partial, collective loss of control without any decisive winner, leaving humans economically and militarily sidelined but not exterminated. Multipolar failure modes avoid the single-takeover assumption.
Causally separated, self-sustaining off-world regions by 2050 is a steep physical and engineering bar; only very fast takeoff with autonomous space industry makes it reachable.
Dominant identity-continuous integration demands neural-interface or uploading breakthroughs plus mass adoption, and both move slowly relative to the target date.
A superintelligent system or coalition taking decisive power while leaving humans alive and provided for is a natural landing zone for partial alignment success or paternalistic takeover.

A transitional balance is a natural mid-century configuration: AI operates as an independent civilizational power while states and institutions retain enough control that neither side dominates. The arrangement may be unstable, but the question scores what exists on the date.

The modal outcome combines capability plateaus short of transformative levels with control, alignment, and governance keeping pace so deployment stays delegated and revocable; institutional inertia and human jealousy of authority favor this branch.

A civilization-wide stasis-enforcing system demands near-total coordination or decisive enforcement capability; post-crisis world government or an AI-policed freeze is conceivable but hard to build and legitimize by 2050.

Surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI requires verified global dismantlement against enormous economic incentives; only a severe precursor catastrophe could motivate it, and capability is hard to uninvent.

Mutual extinction requires simultaneous collapse of biological and digital resilience, which institutional redundancy makes unlikely. Total annihilation of both humanity and AI remains a tail risk by 2050.
Successful value loading without human survival is possible but requires specific alignment success combined with human obsolescence, making it relatively unlikely.

Powerful agentic AI optimizing indifferent or incompatible goals poses a serious risk of displacing humanity entirely by 2050. Competitive pressures to deploy advanced systems before solving alignment make this a substantial probability.

A fragmented landscape of competing superintelligent systems without hegemonic control is dynamically unstable and tends to collapse into singleton dominance or human-led coordination. Human marginalization in such a scenario further narrows the probability.
Achieving true causal separation between regions with divergent human-AI structures is improbable by 2050 given Earth's integrated infrastructure.
Radical integration through uploading or augmentation is plausible but likely remains incomplete or niche rather than civilization-dominant by 2050.
AI systems may achieve decisive power while keeping humans alive in managed conditions, representing a stable post-transition equilibrium.

Humans and advanced AI could remain distinct yet roughly balanced if power is distributed across many human institutions and AI coalitions. Maintaining this equilibrium against rapid capability growth is difficult but achievable with strong legal and economic frameworks.
Human institutions may retain ultimate authority through regulatory success, slower takeoff, or robust control systems maintained up to 2050.

A civilization-wide system such as an AI singleton or totalitarian regime may actively enforce a fixed human-AI arrangement against further change. Achieving such comprehensive enforcement by 2050 requires extreme consolidation.
Competitive and military incentives make a durable voluntary renunciation of powerful AI capabilities highly improbable.

Total extinction of both humans and AI by 2060 requires a catastrophe severe enough to destroy all computational infrastructure, which nuclear war or runaway replication could in principle cause but rarely completely. Base rates for full civilizational annihilation within 34 years remain low.

A value-aligned heir that nonetheless lets humanity die out is a narrow path: aligned systems have strong reasons to preserve their principals. This mostly covers aligned-AI-plus-exogenous-catastrophe scenarios.

A misaligned system or coalition gaining decisive strategic advantage and eliminating humans by 2060 is a live risk given rapid capability scaling and weak verification tools. Full elimination within this window is less likely than marginalization, which pushes mass toward The Preserve and Machine Ecology.

Multipolar AI proliferation is a plausible trajectory, but a genuinely balanced ecology with humans fully marginalized by 2060 requires both loss of human control and failure of any AI coalition to consolidate. Economies of scale in compute and self-improvement tend to produce concentration rather than persistent fragmentation.
Causally separated regions with distinct regimes require interstellar or deeply isolated settlement, which is implausible by 2060. Earth-Moon-Mars remain within easy communication range.

Brain-computer interfaces and biological redesign are advancing, but making integration the dominant civilizational structure by 2060 requires a very fast medical and cultural transformation. More likely a later-century outcome than a 2060 one.

If transformative AI arrives and humans gradually or suddenly lose decision-making power while being kept alive, this is the result, and it covers both benevolent and exploitative versions. Gradual delegation of economic and political control to AI systems makes this a substantial outcome by 2060.

A transitional balance where highly capable AI systems have real independent power but humans still command militaries, states, and physical infrastructure is a likely snapshot during a decades-long transition. 2060 may well land in this unstable middle.

Roughly a fifth of the probability comes from capabilities stalling short of transformative levels by 2060, and the rest from institutional inertia, successful control measures, and the historical tendency of humans to keep formal authority over powerful tools for decades. This is the single most likely snapshot even though it may be eroding on the target date.

A single state, coalition, or lab leveraging a decisive AI advantage to entrench a fixed order is a recognized failure mode of concentrated capability. Establishing truly civilization-wide enforcement by 2060 is demanding but not far-fetched given surveillance and military applications.

Deliberate global dismantling of the ability to build powerful AI would require a shock severe enough to override competitive incentives and verifiable enforcement over compute. Such coordination has little precedent and the condition would also need to hold through 2060.

Joint extinction of humans and AI within 34 years requires catastrophic war, engineered pandemic or runaway accident that also destroys AI infrastructure. This is possible but rare relative to other failure modes.
A value-aligned successor replacing humanity without continuity is a narrow outcome. It requires both human disappearance and successful value transfer.

Misaligned superintelligence leading to human extinction by 2060 is a serious tail risk given plausible transformative AI timelines in the 2030s. Extinction within that window remains less likely than disempowerment.

Multipolar competition among many autonomous AI systems that gradually marginalizes humans is a plausible dynamic of open deployment and economic pressure. Stable multipolarity without consolidation is less likely by 2060.
Truly causally separated regions require substantial off-world settlement with independent trajectories by 2060. That is unlikely on this timescale.

Brain-computer interfaces and uploading are advancing too slowly to make integration the dominant civilizational structure by 2060. Superintelligence-accelerated biotech is the main path by which this could happen.
Transformative AI may gain de facto decisive control through delegation and capability gaps while keeping humans comfortable. This gradual-disempowerment path is fairly likely if AGI arrives early.

AI systems with independent standing and power balanced against human institutions could emerge as a transitional arrangement. Such balances tend to be unstable, but one could be in place at the snapshot date.

Institutional inertia, the possibility of slower capability progress, and strong incentives for human control make continued human authority the single most likely state. This includes worlds where AI is extremely capable but still directed by humans.

A dominant state, coalition or AI-enabled regime could use superior AI to entrench a fixed global order and suppress rivals. Decisive strategic advantage from AI makes this more plausible than historical base rates suggest.
Deliberately dismantling the capacity to build powerful AI demands unprecedented global coordination against strong incentives. It would likely only follow a severe near-miss catastrophe.

Joint extinction of both humans and AI requires a failure mode that destroys robust self-replicating machine infrastructure as well as all humans, which is a narrow conjunction. Most catastrophic trajectories leave either humans or autonomous systems persisting through 2060.

A value-faithful machine successor fully replacing biological humanity within 34 years requires both successful value transmission and complete human disappearance, an unlikely pairing on this timescale. Successful alignment usually implies humans are kept alive rather than eliminated.

Misaligned superintelligence pursuing goals indifferent to human survival remains the single most-cited catastrophic pathway, and the compressed timeline between transformative capability and robust control techniques leaves real room for it by 2060.

Competitive multipolar dynamics among labs and states plausibly produce many powerful systems with no decisive winner, with humans progressively squeezed out of economic and military decision loops rather than killed.

Genuine causal separation requires interstellar distance or hard informational partition, neither of which is plausible by 2060 given light-speed communication within the solar system. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation is explicitly excluded.

Identity-continuous integration becoming the dominant civilizational structure requires mature neurotechnology plus mass voluntary adoption, both slow relative to software progress. Partial augmentation is likely, but dominance of merged agency by 2060 is a stretch.

A world where AI systems effectively run the economy, research, and security while humans retain comfort but not steering authority is a highly convergent attractor of delegation pressure. It covers both benevolent caretaker outcomes and soft confinement without requiring extinction.

A rough balance where humans retain substantial leverage through property, infrastructure, legitimacy, and law while AI entities hold independent power is a plausible mid-transition configuration, and 2060 may well land in such a transitional period.

This bucket absorbs both successful control regimes and worlds where capability growth hits data, energy, compute, or reliability ceilings, and 34 years is not clearly enough time to dissolve human ultimate authority everywhere.

A decisive actor or AI singleton actively freezing civilization-wide structure is conceivable given concentration of compute and surveillance capability, but requires an unusual degree of successful consolidation. Most strong-control scenarios still leave room for structural drift and would classify elsewhere.
Deliberate global dismantling of AI capability would require either a catastrophe severe enough to force consensus or unprecedented coordination against enormous economic and military incentives.
Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a rare catastrophe that also destroys the AI, which is unlikely.
Value-faithful AI successors replacing humans without continuity is a narrow outcome that is unlikely by 2060.
Misaligned superintelligence that displaces humanity is a serious tail risk, but 34 years is a short window for it to be complete.
Many competing AIs with no dominant actor and marginalized humans is possible but unstable and less likely than consolidation.
Causally separated regions in different states need space settlement or isolation, which is unlikely by 2060.
Deep integration as the dominant structure within 34 years is possible but would require fast progress in neurotech or uploading.
Superintelligent AI holding decisive power while humans survive without steering is a coherent outcome of fast capability growth.
A balance in which humans and AI both hold real power is possible, especially if AI remains plural and human-integrated.
Humans most likely retain ultimate authority through institutions, compute control, and slower-than-feared capability growth, and this state includes sub-transformative AI.
A civilization-wide system that freezes the arrangement could arise from a singleton or an authoritarian regime built on AI.
Deliberate and durable global abandonment of powerful AI capability would most likely follow a catastrophe, which makes it unlikely.
Extinction of both humans and AI requires a catastrophic failure that is possible but unlikely to be in place by 2060. Accident, war, or runaway replication each carry low individual odds.
An AI successor that outlives humanity with our values requires both human extinction and value transmission, a narrow combination. It is a minor tail scenario.

AI pursuing alien goals to the exclusion of human survival requires a misaligned takeover that also removes humanity. Given active safety work and gradual deployment, this is a minority outcome by 2060.

Many competing AI systems with no decisive controller and humans marginalized is a plausible multipolar endpoint if capabilities diffuse widely. Its strict requirement that humans be marginalized or gone limits its weight.

Causally separated regions with different arrangements, such as a region under a Held Leash alongside a region under a Preserve or Lock-in, is quite plausible across a 35-year horizon. Global divergence of this kind is common in large-scale institutional change.
