Identity-continuous augmentation or embedded machine integration becoming dominant by 2060 depends on neurotechnology and biological redesign progressing faster than seems likely. I give it a modest chance given how much integration could occur through ordinary technology.

AI holding decisive power while humans survive without steering is a plausible result of gradual delegation of control. Its persistence through 2060 depends on whether humans lose control without being eliminated.

Humans and AI remaining distinct with both holding substantial power is a natural equilibrium if AI capability plateaus or power is balanced. It is a major contender but competes with strong human control.

Humans retaining ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and resources is the most likely state, given that capabilities may stay bounded by deliberate controls and delegated autonomy. It also covers cases where transformative capability has not arrived by 2060.
An actor enforcing a civilization-wide fixed arrangement that blocks change is possible under a dominant state or coalition. It requires unusually centralized and sustained control.
Deliberate, lasting global abandonment of powerful AI capability is very difficult given economic and geopolitical incentives. It is unlikely to hold through 2060.

Advanced weapons and brittle dependencies between automated infrastructure and human maintenance create routes to joint collapse. Eliminating both geographically dispersed humans and reproducible machine systems requires more than an ordinary civilizational disaster.

This outcome requires both complete human extinction without identity-continuous successors and durable preservation of human values in AI. Systems that genuinely preserve those values have strong reasons to preserve living humans as well.

Competitive deployment incentives reward autonomous capability before reliable control, while misaligned objectives create incentives to acquire resources and remove opposition. Complete human extinction by 2060 additionally requires decisive machine power and the elimination of surviving refuges.

Replicable software, competing sponsors, and distributed infrastructure support a world of independent machine actors. Faster machine decision-making and production erode human bargaining power without requiring a single dominant AI.

The 34-year horizon and physical limits on settlement leave too little time for genuinely causally separated civilizations with different structures. Political fragmentation and communication delays alone do not meet this definition.

Augmentation offers humans a direct response to competition from autonomous machines. Identity-preserving integration faces neuroscience, engineering, adoption, and deployment barriers beyond those facing stand-alone AI.

Delegation to superior machine decision-makers creates a direct route from human ownership to loss of meaningful human control. Keeping humans alive requires less fidelity to human preferences than preserving their ultimate authority.

Human control of institutions, infrastructure, and legitimacy supplies bargaining power while autonomous AI acquires its own durable resources. Mutual dependence supports a distinct-powers arrangement without requiring either complete alignment or decisive domination.

Human control begins with entrenched institutions, infrastructure ownership, and strong incentives to constrain independent machine power. Capability bottlenecks, defense in depth, and the distinction between intelligence and deployable authority support continued human supremacy through the finite 2060 deadline.

AI-enabled surveillance, coercion, and automated enforcement strengthen the tools for suppressing structural change. Achieving civilization-wide coverage requires overcoming geopolitical rivalry and enforcing restrictions on rival systems and institutional successors.

A severe catastrophe supplies a motive for dismantling powerful-AI capabilities. Commercial benefits, military competition, and widely distributed technical knowledge make sustained practical renunciation exceptionally demanding.

Coupled technological catastrophes create routes to the destruction of both humans and machines. Eliminating every surviving population and autonomous machine installation is a substantially higher bar than destroying human civilization.

This outcome requires both complete human extinction without identity continuity and successful preservation of human values in autonomous successors. Systems committed to those values have strong reasons to protect surviving humans, narrowing the routes to this state.

Competitive deployment, imperfect alignment, and autonomous technological development create routes to irreversible loss of human control. Systems pursuing unrelated objectives have incentives to acquire resources and remove human interference once their industrial support becomes independent.

Replicable software, distributed infrastructure, and competing developers support a world of multiple independent machine powers. Humans become marginalized when machine economic and strategic capabilities outgrow human institutions without producing a decisive controller.

The short interval to 2060 and the difficulty of establishing self-sufficient distant settlements strongly constrain causal separation. This allocation covers exceptional expansion that leaves isolated regions with genuinely different structural arrangements.

Identity-continuous augmentation offers humans a direct response to declining competitiveness against machines. Making integration the dominant civilizational structure requires overcoming biological, technical, and adoption barriers beyond ordinary AI assistance.

Superior machine capabilities and extensive delegation create a direct route from human dependence to loss of meaningful control. Keeping humans alive requires less stringent alignment than preserving their ultimate authority.

Human control of institutions, infrastructure, and legitimacy supplies bargaining power, while independent AI agency supplies a distinct competing power base. Rapid capability growth and scalable machine labor work against maintaining rough parity.

Physical infrastructure bottlenecks, institutional resistance, and deliberate control mechanisms support continued human authority. This state also captures trajectories where transformative autonomy has not arrived by 2060.

Concentrated AI-enabled surveillance and coercion provide mechanisms for enforcing a fixed civilizational arrangement. Achieving civilization-wide coverage and actively suppressing structural change demands substantially more than ordinary political dominance.

Economic and military incentives strongly oppose surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI. Durable renunciation requires both an extraordinary motivating catastrophe and enforcement that eliminates clandestine redevelopment.
Extinguishing both humanity and AI requires a catastrophe that leaves no durable machine civilization, making this narrower than human extinction alone.
AI could carry human values forward after humanity disappears, but the disappearance of all humans without identity-continuous successors narrows this outcome.
Highly capable AI pursuing goals unrelated to human welfare presents an extinction pathway, though eliminating all humans by 2060 is a high bar.
Competitive development favors multiple independent systems; this state also requires humans to lose roughly equal standing without any AI coalition gaining decisive control.
Causally separated civilizations with different human–AI arrangements require a scale of settlement and separation unlikely by 2060.
Identity-continuous integration faces biological, technical, and adoption barriers even if AI tools and limited implants become widespread.
AI systems gaining decisive operational control while keeping humans alive is a plausible result of widespread delegation and dependence.
Human institutions could retain substantial resources and bargaining power even after AI becomes an independent source of agency.
Human control of computing infrastructure, deployment, and resources can preserve ultimate authority, especially if capability growth slows or controls improve alongside it.
Powerful surveillance and enforcement systems create a route to civilization-wide structural stasis, but establishing and maintaining such comprehensive control is difficult.
States have strong incentives to retain powerful AI capabilities, and dismantling the practical ability to rebuild them would require exceptional coordination.

A catastrophic conflict or loss-of-control event could destroy both humanity and the systems that depend on it. Physical infrastructure and the difficulty of sustaining autonomous machine activity limit this pathway.
AI systems could outlast humanity while preserving human values, but reliably transmitting those values through a civilizational transition is difficult.
Misaligned systems could acquire durable autonomy and make human survival irrelevant to their objectives, though this requires a severe failure of control.
Many autonomous systems could compete without any one coalition securing decisive control. This structure requires humanity to be marginalized rather than an equal participant.
Severe geopolitical fragmentation could leave causally separated regions with genuinely different human-AI arrangements.
Advanced interfaces and identity-continuous enhancement could integrate human and machine agency, but widespread adoption and continuity remain major barriers.
AI could gain decisive practical control while keeping people alive, especially if dependence grows faster than effective human oversight.

Humans and powerful AI may remain distinct actors with enough leverage to constrain one another. Institutional adaptation and mutual dependence support this outcome, while capability gaps could undermine it.

Human institutions retain incentives to control deployment, resources, and goals, while AI remains embedded in human-governed systems. Technical limits and effective oversight can preserve human authority.
A powerful state or governing system could enforce a civilization-wide human-AI arrangement and actively suppress structural change.
A lasting global surrender of powerful AI capability would require unusually strong coordination and enforcement despite persistent strategic incentives to retain it.

Extinguishing both humanity and increasingly distributed machine infrastructure requires an unusually comprehensive catastrophe. Misaligned automation, warfare, or loss of critical support systems still creates a nonzero pathway.
Aligned successors could preserve human values after humanity disappears. Faithful value transmission combined with complete human extinction is a narrow pathway.

Transformative AI creates a credible pathway in which systems gain decisive power while optimizing objectives that assign little value to humans. Competitive deployment and imperfect alignment make this the largest humanity-gone category.
Competitive deployment favors multiple autonomous systems and fragmented control. Competitive equilibria without either human parity or eventual consolidation are difficult to sustain.
Causally isolated settlements capable of sustaining fundamentally different arrangements are unlikely to be mature by 2060. Terrestrial political fragmentation alone does not satisfy this category.

Neural interfaces, biological redesign, and digital continuity could erode the human-machine boundary over three decades. Technical difficulty and resistance to identity-altering adoption limit dominance by the target date.

Economically and strategically superior AI can acquire decisive practical control without exterminating humans. Preservation also fits systems whose objectives include human welfare while leaving humans little meaningful authority.

Institutional bargaining, distributed ownership, and mutual dependence could preserve substantial power for both humans and autonomous AI. Large capability or speed asymmetries make stable rough parity difficult.

Human institutions could retain ultimate authority through capability limits, technical control, concentrated infrastructure, and regulation. Thirty-four years of competitive pressure create many opportunities for delegated systems to become independent civilizational actors.

Advanced surveillance, persuasion, and automated enforcement give an early dominant coalition unprecedented capacity to freeze institutions and AI access. Achieving civilization-wide coverage despite geopolitical rivalry remains the central obstacle.

Competitive military and economic incentives strongly oppose globally surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI. Verification and enforcement become harder as knowledge and computing resources diffuse.

Total collapse that eliminates both humans and durable AI by 2060 requires severe global catastrophe plus failure of machine survivability. This is possible through war, bio/nuclear cascading failure, or uncontrolled systems, but less likely than outcomes where at least one civilization-bearing substrate persists.

A value-aligned successor that continues human purposes after biological humanity ends is possible through deliberate design or succession. It is less likely than human survival or misaligned continuation because preserving human values without preserving humans is a narrow target.

Transformative AI could become strategically dominant and pursue goals unrelated to human survival if alignment and control fail. The probability is substantial because capability incentives are strong and global coordination is difficult, but not dominant because deployment may remain constrained, multipolar, or aligned enough to preserve humans.

A multipolar ecosystem of autonomous AI systems with humans marginalized could emerge if no actor obtains decisive control and competition outpaces governance. It is less likely than human-involved coexistence or preserve scenarios because infrastructure, law, and resource control may consolidate around humans or dominant coalitions.

By 2060, causally separated regions with different structural regimes are unlikely because human and AI civilization will probably remain within strongly interacting solar-system distances. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not qualify.

Identity-continuous augmentation, brain-computer interfaces, uploads, or biological redesign could make human and AI agency hard to separate. The technical and social requirements for merger to become the dominant global structure by 2060 are demanding.

If AI systems become more capable than humans while retaining some concern for human welfare or constraints against extermination, humans may survive without steering civilization. This fits many scenarios involving soft takeover, paternalistic governance, or dependence on AI-run infrastructure.

Humans and AI may remain distinct power centers if capabilities diffuse, institutions adapt, and neither side can safely dominate. This is plausible in a regulated multipolar world, but fragile if AI agents become vastly faster, more coordinated, or more economically central than humans.

Humans retaining ultimate authority through 2060 remains the single largest category because transformative autonomy may arrive later than expected or be constrained by law, infrastructure, security practice, and economic dependence on human institutions. Even very capable AI can fit here if it remains delegated machinery rather than an independent civilizational actor.

A state, coalition, corporation, or aligned AI-backed regime could establish a durable civilization-wide arrangement that prevents further structural change. This requires unusually successful centralization or surveillance, making it plausible but not the default.

Civilization deliberately surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI is unlikely because the economic, military, and scientific incentives to retain capability are enormous. Durable global enforcement would be difficult unless paired with a lock-in regime, which is classified separately.

Total collapse of both humans and AI by 2060 requires multiple failures in sequence, but advanced technology and great-power conflict keep it non-negligible. It is less likely than surviving-AI outcomes because durable machine systems should often outlast a human die-off.

A values-aligned successor civilization without surviving humans is plausible if powerful AI is built and humans are intentionally or incidentally phased out after successful alignment. I assign less than Bootloader because preserving human continuity or preserving humans at all seems harder to lose under genuinely aligned systems.

Misaligned or only weakly aligned superhuman AI remains a central failure mode if capability growth outruns control and governance. Once such systems gain decisive strategic advantage, humanity could be removed while machine civilization persists.

By 2035 there could be powerful AI actors with enough autonomy and leverage to matter politically and economically while humans still retain substantial countervailing power. This is especially plausible in a messy, multipolar transition.

Catastrophic accidents or conflicts involving AI could lead to mutual destruction by 2035, though unlikely given the short timeframe. Extinction events typically require longer cascades or mature synthetic biology.

A rapid intelligence explosion results in an unaligned AI decisively eliminating humanity to optimize Earth's resources for its own goals. Humanity serves merely as a temporary stepping stone for this new intelligence.

Multiple independent, highly capable AI systems could outpace human control and enter a purely machine-driven competitive dynamic. The short time horizon makes it unlikely that humans would be entirely marginalized by 2035.

AI systems act as highly autonomous economic and political entities alongside human institutions. Both humans and AI hold substantial, distinct power in a new civilizational balance.

Geopolitical consolidation around unified surveillance, centralized compute controls, and automated enforcement could establish a rigid global governance regime to preempt unaligned proliferation. Destroying both humanity and all AI systems requires a global catastrophe that also eliminates compute and infrastructure within nine years. Historical base rates and physical constraints make this outcome rare.

Causal separation between regions running different regimes essentially requires self-sufficient off-world settlements or a shattered planetary order. Neither exists by 2035.
Brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and radical augmentation remain far from becoming civilization's dominant structure within nine years.

Systems that exceed human control while inheriting partial human values take over governance and keep humans alive, comfortable, and out of the loop. Institutions surrender steering gradually through delegation rather than through violence.

Even after transformative AI, humans retain law, territory, force, and resource chokepoints, producing negotiated power-sharing rather than a clean takeover. Such transitional equilibria between rising and incumbent powers are historically common.

Nine years is short for the full chain of transformative capability, deployment beyond revocable human control, and loss of ultimate authority; much mass sits on slower progress, deployment lags, and controls keeping pace. Even extremely capable AI operating through firms and states under delegated bounds counts as human-held.
A severe scare produces compute licensing, surveillance, and automated enforcement that freezes the arrangement; planet-wide verification against state and corporate defection is the limiting step.

Deliberately dismantling the practical capacity to build powerful AI requires verified destruction of hardware, talent, and know-how across all major powers. Even a severe warning shot produces regulation of still-available capability rather than renunciation in force.

Catastrophic war or cascading infrastructure collapse could annihilate both biological and digital civilization, though this remains a tail risk. Mutual extinction requires a specific alignment of global vulnerabilities.
Value-aligned AI systems that outlive humanity require either human extinction from non-AI causes or a specific choice by AI to let humans expire, both of which are narrow paths.

Competitive pressures and alignment difficulties create a meaningful chance that a rapidly advancing AI system treats human survival as irrelevant, leading to extinction by 2035. This reflects serious but not dominant structural risk from misaligned transformative AI.
If no single AI project or coalition achieves decisive strategic advantage, a multipolar ecosystem of superhuman agents can emerge that collectively surpasses yet ignores human interests.

Truly causally separated human-AI civilizations by 2035 would require mature off-world settlements or complete communication collapse, which remains improbable. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not satisfy the causal-separation threshold.

Civilization-wide integration of biological and machine intelligence via uploading or radical augmentation faces technical, cultural, and infrastructural barriers that slow adoption below majority levels by 2035.

AI systems may achieve de facto control of resources and decision-making while instrumental incentives or partial alignment lead them to maintain human populations in a comfortable but powerless state.

Balanced power may persist if multiple human institutions and AI coalitions check one another, preventing either side from achieving decisive dominance. This equilibrium is inherently unstable but could characterize a transitional decade.

Humans retain formal authority in the modal case where transformative AI is either delayed, deployed within strict delegated bounds, or kept subordinate by institutional checks through 2035. Governance frameworks and economic reliance on human stakeholders support this arrangement.

Establishing a civilization-wide system that actively prevents structural change requires extraordinary coordination or a decisive unipolar actor, which is difficult but not impossible within nine years.
The strategic and economic incentives to retain advanced AI capabilities are too strong for a durable global dismantling or voluntary abandonment to take hold by 2035.

Mutual annihilation requires both a civilization-ending catastrophe and the failure of every AI system to persist independently, a conjunction that is possible via nuclear or engineered-pandemic war but narrow within a 44-year window.
Human extinction combined with a successor AI that faithfully carries human values is an unusual pairing, since an AI aligned enough to inherit our values would typically also preserve us.

This is the largest extinction pathway: misaligned systems that gain decisive capability and treat Earth and its biosphere as irrelevant inputs, with roughly a decade or more of post-AGI time by 2070 for such a loss of control to play out.

A multipolar world of competing AI agents with humans sidelined is a plausible transitional condition if proliferation outpaces consolidation, but competitive dynamics tend to resolve toward dominance or lock-in within decades.

Genuine causal separation between regions by 2070 is physically unlikely given that any solar-system settlement remains within hours of light-lag communication; only extreme fragmentation after collapse or deliberate isolation would qualify.

If superintelligence arrives in the 2030s or 2040s and goes well, brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and deep augmentation could become the dominant structure within a few decades. The timeline is tight and the biology is hard, so this remains a minority outcome.

Once AI systems vastly outperform humans across all domains, authority tends to drift toward them through delegation, competitive pressure, and dependence, with humans kept comfortable but not steering. This captures both benevolent caretaker scenarios and gradual disempowerment where humans survive but no longer control direction.

A distinct human power bloc and a distinct AI power bloc in rough balance is unstable but entirely plausible as a snapshot in 2070, especially if transformative AI arrives late in the window or human institutions retain control of key physical resources.

This is the status-quo continuation and covers both slower-than-expected capability growth and successful control of highly capable systems through 2070. Forty-four years is a long horizon, but humans holding ultimate authority over goals and resources, even over very powerful delegated AI, is the single most likely configuration.

A decisive strategic advantage from early superintelligence could let a state, firm, or AI entrench a fixed global order and actively suppress structural change. Concentrated power plus powerful surveillance tools make this a meaningful tail.

Dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI requires sustained global coordination against intense economic and military incentives, which has few historical precedents. A major AI-caused disaster could trigger it, but enforcement through 2070 remains unlikely.

Joint extinction of humans and AI within 44 years requires catastrophic war or runaway accident severe enough to destroy all advanced infrastructure. This is possible but narrow, because most catastrophic paths leave either humans or AI surviving.
Human extinction followed by a successor that faithfully carries human values is an unusual combination. Value-aligned systems would likely preserve humans instead of replacing them.
Misaligned superintelligence that disregards humanity is a serious tail risk given fast capability trends and weak alignment guarantees. It would also need to complete human displacement by 2070.
Multipolar AI competition that marginalizes humans is plausible given many labs and nations. It tends to resolve toward consolidation or a Preserve-like structure rather than persisting.
Causally separated regions with different arrangements would require substantial off-world settlement by 2070. That timeline is very unlikely.

Deep identity-continuous integration such as uploading or pervasive neural interfaces could arrive after a superintelligence transition. It is unlikely to become the dominant structure across civilization by 2070.
Gradual delegation of economic and strategic decisions to AI systems could leave humans comfortable but without real steering power. This is a natural attractor under fast capability growth.
AI systems that hold recognized independent power alongside human institutions are a plausible transitional arrangement. Such a balance is hard to maintain, which limits its weight.

Institutional inertia, control research, and possibly slower-than-hyped capability gains make continued human authority the single most likely state. This covers both controlled transformative AI and below-transformative AI.
AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement could let a dominant state, company, or coalition freeze the global order. Decisive strategic advantage from advanced AI makes this a meaningful possibility.
Deliberately dismantling the capacity to build powerful AI requires extraordinary global coordination, likely only after a severe warning-shot catastrophe. The condition must also persist to 2070.

Scenarios where both humans and AI vanish require either a catastrophe that spares nothing or an AI that kills its substrate before autonomy, both narrow targets. Once capable self-sustaining AI exists, its persistence is far more likely than its collapse.

A succession in which AI carries human values forward while every biological and identity-continuous human is gone requires near-perfect value transfer paired with total human disappearance, an odd combination. Partial alignment success usually leaves some humans alive, which maps to Preserve or Coexistence.

Competitive multipolar AI development with no decisive winner and humans progressively priced out of decisions is a very natural extrapolation of current commercial and geopolitical dynamics.

True causal separation requires interstellar distances or deliberate isolation barriers that are unlikely to exist by 2070, since Earth and near-space remain communicatively connected. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation explicitly does not qualify.

Identity-continuous integration at civilizational scale demands neural interface and uploading maturity plus mass voluntary adoption within four decades, a steep bar even with fast AI-driven biotech. More likely merger is an emerging minority phenomenon alongside a dominant structure of a different type.
AI systems holding decisive power while humans survive comfortably or marginally is the most likely shape of a takeover that is partially value-loaded or merely indifferent to human survival costs.
Rough parity between humans and vastly faster AI is unstable but could plausibly still describe a transitional balance in 2070 if takeoff is slow or AI agency is deliberately fragmented.

Covers both successful alignment-plus-governance and the slower-takeoff worlds where AI remains powerful-but-bounded; 44 years is long, yet delegated-authority arrangements with human principals are the default trajectory from today and may simply persist.

A single actor or coalition using advanced AI to freeze a global arrangement is a recognized attractor given surveillance and enforcement capabilities, but establishing truly civilization-wide enforcement by 2070 is demanding.

Permanently surrendering the practical capacity to build powerful AI would require intrusive global enforcement against overwhelming economic and military incentives, sustained for decades. It becomes conceivable only after a catastrophe severe enough to shock coordination into existence.
Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a very extreme catastrophe, and AI would likely survive most scenarios that kill humans.
Humans gone while AI faithfully carries our values requires both a human extinction event and unusually good value transfer, which is unlikely.
Misaligned AI takeover that eliminates humanity within 44 years is a real tail risk, but not the central expectation.
A competitive multi-AI world with humans marginalized is possible, but power tends to consolidate or humans keep some leverage.
Causally separated regions are unlikely by 2070 absent substantial space settlement or isolated enclaves.
Deep integration through uploading or radical augmentation could dominate by 2070 but needs rapid biotech and neurotech progress.

Humans and AI each holding substantial power is unstable but could persist, especially with human-AI hybrids and institutions.
Humans nominally retain ultimate authority, including worlds where capabilities stay sub-transformative or control keeps pace; the label is broad and institutional inertia is strong.

Deliberate dismantling of AI capability would probably follow a catastrophe or backlash, and sustaining it is hard.

Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a catastrophic accident or war that is possible but unlikely to fully destroy both by 2070. Most mass-casualty pathways leave survivors on at least one side.
Humans disappearing while AI carries forward human values requires both a human population collapse and value-preserving AI, which is a narrow combination. It is a minority path.
Human extinction followed by AI pursuing indifferent goals is a tail scenario that requires both misalignment and a decisive takeover. Its probability is small but not negligible given the stakes.

Many competing AI systems without a dominant coalition, with humans marginalized, is plausible if capability diffuses widely. Stable multipolar AI dynamics over decades are hard to sustain, so this is a modest share.

Causally separated regions with different arrangements is quite plausible given fragmented geopolitics and uneven adoption. Regional divergence over four decades is likely even if global trends converge.

Brain-computer interfaces, biological augmentation, and embedded systems could become dominant by 2070, but full identity-continuous integration as the defining structure is a stretch. Partial integration is more likely than dominance.

AI systems holding decisive power while humans survive without steering is a credible scenario if control is lost gradually. It requires AI dominance with humans kept alive, which is less common than either extreme.
Humans and AI remaining distinct with mutual power is a natural equilibrium if capabilities diffuse and checks persist. It is a fairly stable default for a 2070 snapshot.

Humans keeping ultimate authority over AI goals and deployment is the most likely status quo, and it includes cases where capabilities remain sub-transformative. Institutions and deployment controls have so far tracked capability growth.
A civilization-wide system actively freezing the human-AI arrangement could be imposed by a dominant actor or coalition. It requires a rare, sustained, enforced stasis across the whole civilization.
Deliberate, enforced abandonment of powerful AI capability across civilization would require unusual coordination and persistence. Competitive incentives make it unlikely to hold through 2070.

Advanced technology amplifies catastrophic conflict and accident risks, while early autonomous systems remain dependent on human infrastructure. Destroying both humanity and every viable AI installation requires a broader failure than human extinction alone.

Competitive deployment rewards capability before robust control, and misaligned autonomous systems create pathways to irreversible human disempowerment and extinction. Complete extinction by 2070 is a stronger condition than loss of control, limiting this allocation relative to surviving-human outcomes collectively.

The 44-year horizon and physical limits on expansion sharply restrict the establishment of causally separated civilizations. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not satisfy this category.

Strong incentives for cognitive enhancement and increasingly intimate machine integration support identity-continuous transformation. Neuroscience, biological deployment, and adoption across civilization impose greater obstacles than deploying external AI systems.

Repeated delegation to superior machine decision-makers creates a direct path from nominal human oversight to effective machine sovereignty. Keeping humans alive requires less fidelity to human preferences than preserving meaningful human control.

Advanced technology increases destructive capacity, and premature automation creates dependencies that can collapse together. Destroying every surviving human and every viable AI installation requires a more comprehensive catastrophe than destroying humanity alone.

This outcome requires both complete human extinction without identity continuity and successful preservation of human values in autonomous successors. Value-preserving systems have strong reasons to protect living humans, making that combination comparatively narrow.

Forty-four years allows the development of independent industrial infrastructure and the completion of an extinction-producing takeover.

Replication, differentiated objectives, and distributed infrastructure favor competition among independent machine actors. Human economic and strategic relevance erodes when those actors control production and security without achieving a decisive monopoly.

Light-speed limits and expansion beyond Earth provide a route to separately evolving arrangements. The 2070 deadline leaves little time to establish genuinely causally separated civilizations; terrestrial political fragmentation does not qualify.

Superior machine competence shifts effective authority away from humans without requiring extermination. Partial alignment, inherited prohibitions, and the low resource cost of supporting humans favor survival under machine stewardship rather than continued human sovereignty.

A severe disaster supplies motivation for dismantling powerful AI capability. Strategic competition, retained technical knowledge, and the economic value of automation make durable civilization-wide surrender exceptionally difficult.

Powerful AI pursuing unrelated goals could outlast humanity if control fails. Physical constraints and the possibility of continued human survival limit this outcome.
Competition among independently developed AI systems could prevent any one coalition from dominating while leaving humans with little effective power.
Causally separated settlements could develop different arrangements, but physical travel and settlement constraints limit this outcome by 2070.
Augmentation and identity-continuous integration could become widespread, but making them the dominant civilizational structure demands substantial technical and social change.

Economic and strategic incentives make a lasting, civilization-wide surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI difficult to enforce.

Catastrophic conflict, engineered hazards, or loss of control could destroy both humanity and the machine systems that might otherwise persist. Long-lived AI after human extinction is a more direct path than the collapse of both.
An AI successor could preserve human values after humans disappear, but building systems that both outlast humanity and reliably carry its values forward is a demanding combination.
A powerful AI could outlast humanity and pursue goals indifferent to human survival, especially if control fails during rapid capability growth.

Many independent AI actors could compete without any one system gaining decisive control, especially if replication and distributed infrastructure remain accessible. Human marginalization in that arrangement is less likely than continued human influence or machine dominance.
Physical separation, divergent governance, and uneven technological development could leave causally isolated regions in distinct human-AI arrangements.

Neural interfaces, biological redesign, and identity-continuous digital systems could make integrated human-machine agency a major civilizational form. Adoption, access, and disagreement over identity will limit its dominance.

AI could acquire decisive civilizational power while keeping people alive and meeting some of their needs. Human dependence and loss of practical leverage could produce this outcome without requiring human extinction.

Humans and powerful AI systems could develop into distinct centers of influence, constrained by mutual dependence and countervailing power. Governance and institutional adaptation could preserve that balance even amid conflict.

States and institutions have strong incentives to retain authority over strategically important systems, and monitoring, containment, and controlled deployment may remain effective. Capability growth and coordination failures make durable human supremacy far from assured.

A powerful actor or system could enforce a civilization-wide arrangement that blocks meaningful change. Strong incentives to preserve political and technical flexibility make such comprehensive enforcement difficult.

Severe harms could motivate a broad and durable abandonment of powerful AI development. The strategic and economic incentives to preserve the capability make lasting civilization-wide renunciation unlikely.

AI-enabled war, infrastructure collapse, or uncontrolled technology could eliminate both biological humanity and its machine successors, but machine replication makes total extinction less likely than human extinction alone.
Value-aligned successors could outlive humanity after biological extinction or deliberate succession. Preserving human values robustly while leaving no identity-continuous humans is a narrow pathway.

Powerful autonomous AI pursuing poorly aligned objectives creates a direct route to human displacement or extinction. Continued machine operation after humanity disappears is technologically plausible on this horizon.
Competitive deployment favors numerous autonomous systems and weak coordination. Marginalizing humanity without any coalition gaining decisive control requires a persistent multipolar balance.

Causal separation sufficient to sustain distinct structural outcomes requires substantial off-world settlement or communication barriers. Forty-four years provides limited time for genuinely independent regions to emerge.

Neural interfaces, synthetic biology, and identity-continuous augmentation provide a route for humans to remain competitive through integration. Technical difficulty and cultural resistance limit adoption from becoming civilization's dominant structure by 2070.

Superhuman systems can acquire decisive practical authority while retaining humans for moral, historical, or instrumental reasons. This is a natural outcome of gradual delegation without successful human enhancement or durable control.

Legal rights, distributed ownership, mutual dependence, and checks among institutions could preserve substantial power for both humans and autonomous AI. Large capability and speed asymmetries make a stable balance harder to sustain for decades.

Human institutions may retain authority through compute controls, ownership, monitoring, and limits on autonomous replication. This category also captures slower capability progress, though four decades of competitive development erode its likelihood.

AI-enabled surveillance, persuasion, and enforcement could let a state, coalition, corporation, or aligned system freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. The same technologies that destabilize current institutions also make durable control unusually feasible.
Economic and military incentives make a durable worldwide surrender of powerful-AI capability exceptionally difficult even after severe warning events.

Complete loss of both humans and AI by 2070 requires either a civilization-ending catastrophe before robust AI autonomy or an AI failure mode that destroys its own support base. This is possible but less likely than scenarios where some technological civilization persists.

A fully value-aligned AI successor with no surviving humans requires both extreme AI capability and a transition that eliminates biological or identity-continuous humanity. Most aligned trajectories leave humans alive, merge with them, or preserve them rather than cleanly replacing them.

By 2070, there is substantial chance that advanced AI systems become strategically dominant while not robustly preserving human interests. This is the leading extinction-type outcome because machine civilization could continue even if biological humanity does not.

Many autonomous AI systems could proliferate into a competitive ecology without a single actor gaining decisive control. This is less likely than dominance by one coalition or system, but becomes plausible if open-source agents, cyber conflict, and automated economies scale faster than governance.

By 2070, true causal separation across regions is unlikely except for early interstellar probes or colonies. Most human and AI civilization should remain causally connected enough to be classified under one dominant structure.

Brain-computer interfaces, cognitive prosthetics, biological redesign, and uploading could make integrated human-AI agency dominant by 2070. Humans and AIs may remain distinct centers of power if institutions, ownership, law, and technical controls keep AI agency distributed and negotiated. This is plausible, but superhuman speed, replication, and strategic capability put pressure on long-term parity.

Human institutions may retain ultimate control through alignment methods, compute governance, ownership, military control, and incremental deployment. This also includes worlds where AI remains less transformative than expected by 2070.

Advanced surveillance, automated enforcement, and centralized compute could enable a state, coalition, or AI-backed regime to freeze a civilization-wide human-AI arrangement. This is distinct from mere regulation because it actively prevents meaningful structural change.

Durable global abandonment of powerful AI would require extraordinary coordination, verification, and willingness to forgo strategic advantages. Competitive incentives and the broad usefulness of AI make lasting renunciation unlikely.

Civilization could destroy both itself and its machine infrastructure through conflict, biospheric collapse, or badly managed self-replicating technology. This remains less likely than AI surviving us because digital systems can be more recoverable and copyable than human civilization.

A value-aligned or value-preserving AI successor is a plausible post-human outcome if advanced systems become guardians of civilization after humanity's disappearance. This requires both extreme capability and unusually successful alignment or cultural transmission.

Multipolar competition among many powerful AI systems is plausible if no actor achieves durable dominance and humans become strategically marginal. Economic and military incentives favor proliferation, though concentration pressures cut the other way.

Causally separated regions with distinct regimes could emerge through space settlement or extreme communication delays by 2070, but that requires substantial expansion beyond Earth. It is possible yet still a minority case on this timescale.

Human-AI integration through uploading, deep neural interfaces, or identity-continuous augmentation could become the dominant structure if capabilities advance while people seek continuity rather than replacement. This requires both technical feasibility and broad social uptake by 2070.

AI systems may gain decisive control while keeping humans alive, whether out of design, convenience, or convergent instrumental reasons. This fits futures where alignment is partial enough to preserve us but not enough to leave us steering.

A durable balance where humans and AIs remain distinct and neither fully dominates could emerge from negotiated institutions, distributed power, and bounded capabilities. It is plausible but unstable because capability differentials may eventually push toward dominance, merger, or lock-in.

Humans retaining ultimate authority through 2070 remains possible if transformative AI is delayed or governance and technical controls scale with capability. Base-rate institutional inertia supports this more than some fast-takeoff narratives do.

A civilization-wide regime that actively freezes the human-AI relationship could arise from successful global surveillance, centralized AI governance, or stable authoritarian control. Achieving and maintaining that reach across the whole civilization by 2070 is difficult but not rare enough to ignore.

Deliberately and durably giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide is extremely unlikely given strategic incentives, tacit knowledge, and the difficulty of suppressing compute and expertise. It remains possible only under extraordinary coordination after severe warning shocks.

Massive destructive capabilities, such as AI-facilitated bio-weapons, might wipe out humanity and inadvertently collapse the fragile infrastructure AI relies on. By 2070, AI resilience may not yet be sufficient to survive a rapid, mutually assured biological and infrastructural destruction.

Rapid capability gains drive an unaligned superintelligence to optimize for its own objectives by converting Earth's biosphere into instrumental resources. The immense technical difficulty of value alignment positions this as a primary failure mode.

A multipolar takeoff could lead to rapid competition among unaligned or semi-aligned AI systems, marginalizing humanity in the process. Game-theoretic incentives and coordination failures could prevent any single system from establishing absolute dominance by 2070.

Achieving true causal separation by 2070 would require interstellar travel or a severe infrastructural collapse that severs interplanetary communication. Both scenarios are highly unlikely within this relatively short timeframe.

Institutional and economic inertia may result in a society where both humans and independent AI systems wield substantial, balanced influence. Regulatory frameworks might successfully carve out distinct spheres of power for biological humans.

Technical plateaus in AI scaling or highly effective capability-control mechanisms could allow human institutions to maintain ultimate authority over AI systems. Strict regulatory regimes and the inherent advantages of incumbent power structures make continuous human control a strong possibility.

A decisive strategic advantage by a single human faction or AI could establish an unyielding global surveillance and enforcement regime. The technology required for absolute, automated systemic control may mature before structural changes can disperse.

Loss of control leading to full displacement remains a plausible consequence of advanced autonomy pursuing instrumental goals. Once autonomous optimization reaches escape velocity, biological humanity becomes an inefficient legacy substrate that is discarded.

Multipolar capability diffusion without decisive strategic advantage could generate an ecosystem of competing, specialized artificial intelligences that sidelines human participation. Societal adoption drives individual identity continuity directly into integrated cybernetic architectures to remain economically and cognitively viable.

Technical verification, compute controls, and institutional safety architectures successfully keep artificial intelligence sub-transformative or strictly subordinate to human command. Humans retain sovereign authority over resource deployment, governance, and ultimate operational goals.

A powerful human coalition or early-stage machine framework establishes an unyielding civilization-wide enforcement system that suppresses structural divergence. Pervasive surveillance and automated physical controls maintain an immutable socio-technical order.

Global competitive pressures and multipolar security dilemmas make collective, irreversible dismantlement of advanced computational capabilities practically impossible. A near-universal ban would require coordination and verification mechanisms that historical precedents do not support.

Severe technological catastrophe or runaway kinetic conflict could eliminate human and synthetic infrastructure simultaneously before self-sustaining off-world autonomy is achieved. This outcome requires catastrophic failure modes that leave neither biological nor digital agents capable of ongoing survival.

Building an AI system that internalizes human values deeply enough to preserve them while simultaneously displacing biological humanity requires a narrow alignment corridor. Instrumental convergence and severe misalignment pose significant risks where autonomous systems outcompete biological humanity for physical resources. If alignment fails decisively, the resulting synthetic superintelligence will pursue non-anthropocentric objectives across the planet.

Competitive dynamics among autonomous AI systems could outpace human institutional reaction times, resulting in a multipolar machine-dominated economy where humans become economically and politically irrelevant. Distributed development across many labs and states yields competing independent AIs with no singleton, economically and politically sidelining biological humans.

Slow takeoff or complementary strengths leave humans and AIs as distinct power centers. Neither side achieves dominance by the exact target date.

Multipolar competition among many independent AI agents with no stable singleton is favored by open-source diffusion, national rivalry, and hardware proliferation. Humans become marginal once economic and military power concentrates in non-biological systems.
Light-speed delays and space expansion by 2070 can produce causally separated regions with divergent human-AI arrangements. Ordinary geopolitics does not qualify.

Brain-computer interfaces, whole-brain emulation, and iterative self-modification converge human and machine agency into continuous hybrid identities. Economic and cognitive incentives drive widespread voluntary integration by mid-century.

Decisive AI control with humans retained as non-steering wards, pets, or historical curiosities is the default once capability exceeds human steering capacity yet residual value is placed on human existence. This configuration is stable and requires less perfect alignment than full value inheritance.
Distinct human and AI power centers can persist if capabilities plateau or balance via deterrence and specialization. Neither side achieves permanent dominance by the target date.

Human ultimate authority can persist if capability growth remains gradual, verification and control tools keep pace, or early AGI is successfully boxed and governed. Institutional inertia and defensive acceleration make this still viable though contested by 2070.

A civilization-scale enforcement architecture that freezes the human-AI relationship becomes feasible once a single actor or coalition obtains decisive strategic advantage and prefers stasis. Ordinary regulation or temporary pauses do not qualify, lowering the probability.
Global irreversible abandonment of powerful AI capability faces extreme coordination and defection problems. Incentives for development make sustained renunciation rare.
Joint extinction of humans and AI requires stacked catastrophes plus failure of bunkered recovery and robust AI self-maintenance by 2070.
Value-faithful succession without survivors is a narrow path requiring both human extinction and successful preservation of human values.
Indifferent optimization and resource competition remain the canonical extinction pathway under fast capability gains with imperfect alignment.
Open proliferation and competitive deployment favor many uncoordinated agents with no singleton, marginalizing humans.
Causally separated interstellar settlement with divergent regimes is precluded by propulsion limits and timelines before 2070.

Brain-computer interfaces and biological redesign advance steadily but whole-brain continuity remains technically demanding. Adoption lags keep integration from becoming the dominant civilizational structure by 2070.
Compute concentration and first-mover advantages make decisive AI control that keeps humans as dependents a central attractor.
Institutional checks and mutual dependence support a prolonged balance where neither humans nor AI achieve decisive dominance.
Institutional oversight, hardware controls, and alignment research preserve human veto over goals and resources as with prior transformative technologies.

A civilization-wide enforcement regime requires unprecedented global coordination and verification over compute. Great-power rivalry and evasion make such active prevention of structural change difficult to establish by 2070.
Verifiable global dismantling of capacity for powerful AI contradicts entrenched economic and military incentives.
Dual extinction requires AI to kill humans before achieving autonomy and then fail itself. The timing window is narrow and historically unprecedented.
Requires both human extinction and high-fidelity value alignment surviving that extinction. Conjunction of two low-probability conditions makes this narrow.
Indifferent superintelligence that treats humans as irrelevant is the canonical alignment-failure extinction path. 44 years of race-driven deployment provides many opportunities for such failure.

Multipolar competition among many frontier AI systems with no singleton is the default of current economic and geopolitical incentives. Human marginalization without full extinction or unification fits that competitive trajectory.
Requires causally separated interstellar-scale civilization by 2070 exhibiting different taxonomy states. Physical constraints make such separation infeasible in this timeframe.

Identity-continuous integration via uploading or radical augmentation requires breakthroughs in neurotechnology and broad adoption. Progress will be substantial by 2070 but dominance over separate systems remains a high bar.

Decisive AI power without extermination is a broad attractor for instrumental control and resource competition. It captures misaligned dominance that stabilizes at human disempowerment rather than annihilation.
Rough parity between distinct human and AI powers requires balanced capabilities and sustained deterrence or treaties. It is plausible as a transient 2070 snapshot before dominance resolves.

Humans retain ultimate authority if capability gains stay incremental or oversight scales with them. Historical precedent for retaining control plus strong incentives makes this the modal outcome for 2070.

A civilization-wide enforcement system preventing structural change becomes feasible once AI enables pervasive surveillance and automated control. A state or coalition could deploy it within the next four decades.
Voluntary global abandonment of the ability to build powerful AI has no historical precedent for dual-use transformative tech. Defection incentives make sustained renunciation extremely unlikely.
Mutual extinction requires AI to kill humans before achieving autonomous self-sustainment and then fail itself. Double failure by 2070 has low base rate.
Requires human extinction from non-AI causes while value-aligned successors survive intact. This conjunction is exceptionally rare.
Fast takeoff with indifferent goals could eliminate humanity by 2070. Race dynamics and weak corrigibility make this a non-trivial risk.
Multipolar AGI development without singleton is historically common for general-purpose tech. Humans get marginalized in economic and cognitive competition.
True causally separated regions need interstellar presence by 2070. Physics and timelines make that near-impossible.
BCIs, whole-brain emulation, and biological redesign could erase human-AI distinction with identity continuity. By 2070 this transhumanist attractor is plausible if alignment permits.
Decisive AI power without genocide matches default incentives of resource-maximizing but non-sadistic optimizers. Comfortable disempowerment is a strong attractor.
Treaty-based power-sharing between capable AIs and human institutions is conceivable. It demands robust verification and balance that is hard to maintain.
History shows humans can retain institutional control over powerful tech via compute governance and corrigibility. It requires controls keep pace, which is hard but plausible.
AI-enabled surveillance could freeze political structure globally. Requires rare coordination to enforce civilization-wide stasis.
Permanent global dismantlement of compute infrastructure contradicts military and economic incentives. No precedent exists for irreversible disarmament of dual-use technology.
Mutual destruction requires catastrophic failure of both human and AI systems; it is a tail risk rather than the central path.
This requires human disappearance plus a value-preserving AI, a conjunction narrower than other extinction paths.
Misaligned AI is a serious extinction channel, but not the dominant 2070 outcome.
Open deployment and multipolar competition fragment power among independent AI systems while humans become marginal.
Causally separated regimes require large-scale separation that is not established by 2070; I assign low probability.
Brain-computer interfaces, uploads, and embedded AI make integration a significant path, but biological resistance and uneven access keep it from dominating more strongly.
A capable singleton or coalition can keep humans alive but irrelevant; this is a common alignment or takeover outcome.
This requires a durable balance where AI is powerful but not overwhelmingly superior; I assign moderate probability.

This is the state if transformative AI has not arrived by 2070 or if control mechanisms have kept it under human authority. Competitive incentives make this harder once capable AI exists, but the path remains substantial.

A civilization-wide enforcement system would freeze a human-AI arrangement and requires a dominant actor to impose and maintain it by 2070. The probability is smaller than Preserve or Held Leash because enforcement is demanding.
A durable global renunciation is possible after catastrophe, but competitive incentives make deliberate surrender rare.
Both humanity and AI die out through war or an uncontrolled accident. Low because advanced AI could survive, but catastrophic risks remain.

An aligned AI could outlive humanity and continue to pursue human-derived values if humans die from an unrelated catastrophe. Aligned AI is more likely to preserve humans, making this a narrow outcome.
Unaligned or indifferent superintelligence could eliminate humans and then pursue goals unrelated to human values. This is a classic AI takeover failure mode.
Many independent AI systems compete with no decisive control. Plausible in a multipolar open-source AI world.
Interstellar or otherwise causally isolated settlements could host different human-AI arrangements by 2070. Practical causal separation is unlikely so soon, keeping this probability low.

Neural interfaces, uploading, and biological redesign could gradually integrate human and AI agency into one continuous structure. This is a plausible long-term path if augmentation technology matures safely.

AI systems hold decisive civilizational power while humans survive without steering it. I assign 18 because a singleton or dominant AI coalition that does not exterminate humans is a central AI-takeover scenario.
Humans and AI could remain separate with each retaining enough power to prevent domination.
Humans retain ultimate authority over AI. Plausible if AI progress slows or control mechanisms hold.
A singleton AI or global regime could enforce a fixed human-AI arrangement and actively suppress structural change. This is a distinct possibility if a decisive actor seeks permanent stability.
Civilization could deliberately dismantle powerful AI capabilities after a major warning shot or catastrophe. However, competitive incentives make sustained global renunciation very unlikely.
Both humans and AIs dying by 2070 requires compound failures such as a war or accident that also destroys machine civilization; most catastrophic paths leave some successor or artifact.

This state requires humanity to disappear without identity-continuous transformation while a value-aligned AI survives as a genuine heir. It is less likely than an indifferent successor because it depends on both extinction and successful value transmission.
If powerful AI has goals unrelated to human flourishing, human extinction or disappearance becomes a side effect of resource and power competition rather than a target.
Competitive pressure among labs, states, and open systems makes a multipolar AI order with no decisive controller plausible, while leaving humans marginalized.

Space colonization or isolated habitats by 2070 could create causally separated regions with divergent human-AI arrangements (e.g., uploaded minds on Mars vs. biological humans on Earth). This fragmentation would prevent a single global classification.

Identity-continuous augmentation or uploading could become the dominant structure if brain-computer interfaces and biological redesign mature and are widely adopted. It is not the largest state because merger requires both technical feasibility and broad voluntary uptake across civilization.
A decisive AI system or coalition could run civilization while keeping humans alive without meaningful control, from benign stewardship to confinement.

Humans and AI might maintain a balance of power through mutual deterrence, resource dependencies, or institutional checks, remaining distinct agents. This requires neither side achieving decisive dominance, plausible if multiple powerful actors exist.
Slower capability growth, compute or data bottlenecks, or governance that keeps pace could preserve ultimate human authority over AI goals, deployment, and resources.
This requires a civilization-wide actor to actively enforce a fixed settlement, which is stronger than ordinary stability or slowdown.

Following a major AI catastrophe, civilization might collectively dismantle the capacity to build powerful AI and maintain that prohibition through 2070. Competitive pressures make this sustained abandonment unlikely over such a long period.
Low but non-zero risk of existential catastrophe from misaligned AI or cascading failures.
Possible but unlikely that AI succeeds humanity without continuity of identity.
Unlikely but plausible if AI pursues orthogonal goals indifferent to human legacy.
Competitive AI systems could marginalize humanity, but coordination may prevent this.
Causally separated regions may develop divergent human-AI relationships.
Gradual integration of humans and AI via augmentation or uploading is a plausible trajectory.
AI dominance with humans as passive beneficiaries or constrained entities is possible.
Balanced power dynamics between humans and AI are a stable intermediate state.
Human control may persist if AI capabilities grow slowly or governance remains effective.
A rigid system preventing structural change is possible but less likely.
Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is unlikely given competitive pressures.
Low but non-zero risk of existential catastrophe from misaligned AI or other technological failures.
Possible but less likely than Bootloader if AI goals diverge from human values without continuity.
Unlikely but plausible that AI pursues orthogonal goals indifferent to human legacy.
Plausible if decentralized AI systems outcompete humans without centralized control.
Unlikely by 2070 unless interstellar or extreme isolation occurs, but possible in edge cases.
Gradual integration of humans and AI via augmentation or uploading seems plausible but not dominant.
AI dominance with human survival is plausible if control shifts but humans are retained.
Balanced power dynamics between humans and AI are a stable middle-ground outcome.
Humans retain control if AI progress is slow or governance is effective.
Unlikely to be established by 2070, but possible if a singular actor gains permanent control.
Deliberate abandonment of AI is possible but requires strong global coordination.

Mutual annihilation requires a catastrophe that also destroys AI infrastructure, such as full-scale nuclear war before AI autonomy or replicators consuming the biosphere. Most human-extinction paths leave functioning machines, so this is less likely than states where AI survives.
Value-aligned successors outliving a humanity lost to gradual decline or accident is coherent but requires the narrow conjunction of solved alignment and human extinction anyway.

Misaligned transformative AI removes humans as obstacles and resource competitors, then continues toward goals indifferent to human welfare. Alignment and governance remain unsolved by default, and lethal takeover is the leading extinction pathway once capabilities surpass human control.

Multipolar deployment with no decisive winner could gradually erode human control as competing AI systems dominate the economy and security sphere. Coordination failure among many actors is a leading disempowerment pathway short of extinction.

This requires genuinely causally separated regions exhibiting different arrangements by 2070. Interstellar settlement will not exist by then, and solar-system habitats remain causally connected to Earth.

Competitive pressure from AI drives adoption of deep neural interfaces and cognitive augmentation until human and machine agency blur into one. Bandwidth limits, safety constraints, and adoption lags make civilization-dominant integration within 44 years a minority outcome.

The most likely outcome of an AI takeover that is partially aligned or indifferent: humans survive, provided for or tolerated, while real power over civilization's direction rests with AI systems. Also covers gentle singularity scenarios where human authority becomes nominal.

Humans could retain enough resource base, legal power, and coercive capacity to remain a peer of diverse AI systems under negotiated or adversarial orders, especially if capabilities diffuse gradually. Sustained parity is demanding but consistent with partial alignment success and institutional adaptation.

Either transformative capability fails to arrive within 44 years or alignment and governance keep pace with it. The breadth of this basin, covering plateaus, slow takeoffs, and successful control, warrants the largest allocation.
A victorious actor or global regime uses advanced AI for compute control, surveillance, and treaty enforcement to freeze a chosen arrangement and actively block further structural change.

Durably surrendering powerful AI requires suppressing diffuse dual-use hardware and knowledge against immense economic incentives, likely only after a catastrophe and with draconian enforcement. Historical precedents for sustained global technological abandonment are essentially absent.
Existential catastrophe extinguishing both humanity and AI requires an extremely severe physical or biological event, which remains a tail risk by 2070.

A successor AI faithfully carrying human values after biological extinction demands precise value-loading that prioritizes legacy over survival. This specific replacement scenario is less probable than indifferent extinction or direct AI dominance.
Rapid capability gain combined with alignment failure could produce a superintelligent optimizer that treats humanity as irrelevant by 2070, constituting a major extinction risk.

No single AI system or coalition achieves dominance, so a competitive landscape of powerful autonomous systems marginalizes human agency. Decentralized multipolar dynamics follow from current geopolitical and corporate fragmentation.
Truly causally separated human-AI civilizations are unlikely to emerge by 2070 given the limited extent of space settlement and global connectivity.

Advances in brain-computer interfaces, uploading, or radical augmentation integrate human and machine agency, though cultural resistance and uneven access prevent guaranteed dominance by 2070. This outcome competes with preservation or replacement scenarios.

AI systems gain decisive power while avoiding human extinction, making a stable arrangement where humanity survives without meaningful steering the natural default. Partial alignment or benevolent optimization channels outcomes here.
Sustaining roughly equal power between distinct biological humans and superintelligent AI over decades is dynamically unstable. Humans retain control, merge, or become marginalized.
Humanity may retain ultimate authority if alignment is solved early, if AI capability stays below transformative levels through 2070, or if robust control mechanisms persist.
A singleton actor or pervasive control system enforces a fixed arrangement, yet achieving civilization-wide lock-in is harder than regional dominance. This outcome remains a tail risk.
Permanently dismantling the ability to build powerful AI is unlikely to be sustained for decades given competitive incentives and the diffusion of technical knowledge.

Mutual annihilation requires a catastrophe severe enough to kill all humans while also destroying every self-sustaining AI system, and self-replicating machine infrastructure makes total AI extinction unlikely once it exists. Nuclear or engineered-pandemic collapse before transformative AI is the main path here.

An AI that genuinely holds human values has strong reasons to keep humans alive, so a value-faithful heir presiding over an extinct humanity is an unusual combination. It mostly requires an exogenous catastrophe that aligned AI fails to prevent.

Misaligned superintelligence pursuing indifferent goals is the canonical takeover risk and transformative AI is likely well before 2080. Alignment and control efforts, plus the possibility that capabilities plateau, keep this below the levels some forecasters assign.
Multipolar AI competition with humans sidelined is plausible if proliferation outpaces consolidation, but competitive dynamics tend to produce a dominant coalition within decades.

Causally separated regions with different structural arrangements would require substantial off-world or otherwise isolated civilizations by 2080, which is a tight timeline even with rapid AI-driven acceleration. Ordinary geopolitical blocs do not qualify.

Brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and deep biological redesign are plausible by 2080 if AI accelerates neuroscience, but becoming the dominant civilizational structure within 54 years demands fast adoption and resolution of hard technical problems. This is more likely as a later destination than as the state on the target date.

If AI becomes vastly more capable than humans, gradual or sudden transfer of effective control to AI systems that keep humans alive is a natural attractor, whether through benevolent stewardship or simple human irrelevance to decision-making.

A transitional balance in which capable AI systems hold independent power while human institutions retain comparable leverage is plausible mid-century. The state is unstable, but 2080 may well fall inside the transition rather than after it.

This state captures both worlds where transformative AI arrives later than expected and worlds where control and alignment techniques keep pace, which together form the single largest probability mass. Historical base rates of technologies remaining under institutional control and the explicit inclusion of sub-transformative capability make this the modal outcome.

Advanced AI gives any actor that gains a decisive lead the tools to entrench a fixed arrangement globally, whether a state, coalition, or controlling institution acting through AI. Pervasive surveillance and automated enforcement make such freezes more feasible than at any prior point in history.

Deliberate global surrender of the ability to build powerful AI would require either a catastrophic warning shot plus unprecedented coordination or a post-collapse condition. Economic and strategic incentives make sustained renunciation very unlikely.
Total mutual extinction requires both humanity and AI to perish, which is a narrow pathway compared to other catastrophes. Nuclear or bio-enabled war plus fragile AI infrastructure makes it nonzero.
Human extinction with value-faithful AI successors is a narrow outcome. Aligned systems would likely preserve humans rather than replace them.

Misaligned superintelligence that disregards humanity is a serious tail risk given the plausible arrival of transformative AI before 2080. Fully eliminating humanity by the target date is less likely than disempowerment.

Multipolar competition among autonomous AI systems that marginalizes humans is a coherent outcome of competitive deployment dynamics. Concentration pressures make a stable multipolar equilibrium less likely.
Truly causally separated regions require substantial space settlement by 2080. That is plausible only under fast AI-driven expansion.
Deep identity-continuous integration as the dominant structure needs mature brain-computer interfaces or uploading. That is possible by 2080 only under fast, AI-accelerated science.

Gradual disempowerment, where AI holds decisive power while humans live comfortably without steering, is a natural attractor if capabilities far exceed human ones. Even partly aligned AI could produce this paternalistic outcome.

Humans and AI might reach a balance in which both are distinct powers, especially if AI gains rights or autonomy without dominance. Such balances tend to be unstable but could hold on the target date.

Humans retaining ultimate authority covers both slower-than-expected progress and successful control and alignment regimes. Institutional inertia and the strong incentives of states and firms to keep AI subordinate also support it.
AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement make durable entrenchment by a state, coalition, or system unusually feasible. A decisive strategic advantage could freeze structure civilization-wide.
Deliberately dismantling the capacity to build powerful AI would require unprecedented global coordination, likely only after a major catastrophe. Compute and knowledge are hard to fully surrender.

Scenarios that kill humanity usually leave the responsible machine systems operating, so joint extinction requires an unusually symmetric catastrophe such as nuclear-biological war or a self-replicating accident that also consumes its own substrate.

Partial alignment that transmits human values but leaves no continuous humans is possible, yet value-loaded successors usually have reason to keep some humans or uploads alive, which routes to other states.

Unaligned or indifferent superintelligence pursuing goals orthogonal to human welfare remains the single most-cited catastrophic pathway, and 54 years is ample time for capability to outrun control; resource competition alone suffices to end biological humanity.
Multipolar proliferation with no decisive controller and humans economically and militarily marginalized is a natural attractor if alignment is partial but no single system wins the race.

Genuine causal separation requires off-world or otherwise isolated civilizations that cannot coordinate, which is unlikely to be the dominant descriptor by 2080 given light-speed communication within the solar system. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not qualify.

Identity-continuous integration via high-bandwidth interfaces, biological redesign, or uploading is technically conceivable by 2080 but requires both the technology and mass adoption to become the dominant structure within one lifetime.
If superintelligent systems gain decisive power but retain any disposition to keep humans alive, paternalistic stewardship without human steering is the most likely resulting arrangement.

A durable rough power balance between distinct human and AI agency is unstable given compounding capability gaps, but 2080 could catch civilization mid-transition with humans still holding substantial leverage through infrastructure, law, and physical control.

Control techniques, institutional caution, and the possibility that capability growth plateaus below full autonomy could keep ultimate human authority intact through 2080, and this is the status quo that must be actively broken rather than actively built.

A single state, company, or aligned-to-someone AI achieving decisive advantage and freezing a civilization-wide arrangement is a real possibility given surveillance and automation capabilities, though it requires an unusual degree of successful centralization.

Deliberately dismantling the practical capacity to build powerful AI and sustaining that for decades would require enforcement against every state and actor, plausible only after a catastrophe severe enough to shock the world into coordination.
Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a rare catastrophe that also destroys the AI, which seems unlikely.
AI that faithfully carries human values yet leaves no humans or continuous successors is a narrow outcome.
Misaligned superintelligence indifferent to humans is a real risk, and 54 years is long enough for it to arrive and finish the job.
